author: groundxero
title: Amid Ongoing Siang Protests, In-Principle Forest Clearance Nod to Naying Hydroelectric Project; Over One Lakh Trees to Be Felled
content:
The recommendation for in-principle forest clearance for the 1,000-MW Naying Hydroelectric Project in Arunachal Pradesh comes amid escalating protests against large dam projects in the Siang river basin.

With 470.8 hectares of forest land set to be diverted, compensatory afforestation proposed 1,700 kilometres away in Madhya Pradesh, and landowners rejecting NEEPCO’s compensation offer, the

Naying

project on the Siyom River raises serious questions about ecological destruction, and the social cost of hydropower expansion

in a region where indigenous communities are increasingly resisting such projects that threaten their forests, rivers and ancestral lands.


 


Groundxero


Desk


 


Amid growing opposition and resistance to the proposed 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh, another major hydroelectric project in the Siang river basin has moved closer to implementation. On October 23, 2026, the Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) of the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

recommended in-principle forest clearance

 for the 1,000-MW Naying Hydroelectric Project on the Siyom River (Yomgo River), a major tributary of the Siang.


 


The FAC recommendation permits the diversion of 470.8 hectares of unclassed forest land for the project, which will require the felling of approximately 1,04,036 trees. The FAC has categorised the project area as a “high conservation value zone”. The clearance comes despite persistent objections from project-affected communities, unresolved disputes over land compensation and allegations of procedural irregularities in the environmental clearance process.


 


The Naying project, being developed by the North Eastern Electric Power Corporation (NEEPCO), is a run-of-the-river scheme with peaking power generation capability. Proposed on the Siyom (Yomgo) River, a right-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra, the project extends across parts of Shi-Yomi and Siang districts, both bordering China. With an estimated investment of Rs 11,835 crore, it involves the construction of a 108-metre-high concrete gravity dam over an area of approximately 470 hectares.


 


The project was conceived more than a decade ago and received the Central Electricity Authority’s concurrence in 2013. Its progress remained stalled for years because of environmental and social concerns, particularly the large-scale diversion of forest land. The Union Environment Ministry’s Expert Appraisal Committee recommended environmental clearance in June 2026, and the project received conditional environmental clearance in July. The conditions included safeguards relating to compensatory afforestation, wildlife conservation, air and noise pollution monitoring, and waste management. A mandatory public hearing was subsequently held at Yapik village in Shi-Yomi district.


 


Construction is expected to begin around 2028, with commissioning targeted for 2032.


 


Landowners reject NEEPCO’s compensation offer


 


The successive clearance procedures of the project have intensified opposition among affected landowners. Twelve villages are expected to be affected, and grievances over compensation have developed into a major source of conflict between local communities and NEEPCO.


 


The dispute reached a deadlock in September 2026, when NEEPCO proposed compensation of just Rs 130 per square metre for land and forest resources during an administrative meeting in Yapik village. The Naying Hydroelectric Project Land Owner Welfare Committee (NHEPLOWC), led by its chairman, Taya Yabu, rejected the offer, describing it as a gross undervaluation of ancestral land.


 


The landowners pointed out that compensation rates for comparable infrastructure projects in other districts of Arunachal Pradesh ranged between Rs 3,000 and Rs 5,000 per square metre. They demanded that the same standard be applied to the Naying project.


 


On September 23, landowners from seven affected villages met at Yapik and formally decided to suspend all cooperation with NEEPCO until their demands concerning compensation and land rights were addressed.


 


The nine-point memorandum submitted by the Land Owner Welfare Committee also raised objections to unauthorised tree cutting and clear-felling within designated local forest areas without the required final clearances and compliance procedures.

author: Kodao Productions
title: IBON to Marcos: Explain worst inflation rate in 18 years
content:
IBON Foundation executive director Sonny Africa dared the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to explain why the Philippines has the highest inflation rate in Southeast Asia.


Reacting to Malacañang’s claim Marcos is “doing something” about soaring prices of commodities, Africa said the president’s inaction is behind the people’s worst poverty and hunger in decades.


“It’s because Malacañang’s ‘doing something’ is just enough for a press release, and far less than what’s needed and what it can do,” Africa said.


The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) announced his week that the country’s inflation rate worsened further in October at 7.8 per cent, up from September’s 7.2 per cent.


Marcos in late September assured his government is doing everything it can to keep the economy stable despite heavy pressures from external factors, , including rising global oil prices.


“Do not take it with alarm. Don’t panic,” Marcos said in September.


All images from Africa’s Facebook post.


But Africa asked if Malacañang doing enough, reminding government that the poorest and most vulnerable are ever the ones hit the worst.


“But then these figures probably really are just numbers and nothing to panic about for those like the president, his Cabinet, the economic managers, BSP officials, and trapo allies. It’s a little different if you’re earning millions of pesos annually, and have wealth running into the billions,” he said.


Marcos and wife Liza Araneta are reportedly worth nearly P1.5 billion.


Try living on P96 a day


The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP), meanwhile, challenged Marcos and fellow officials to live on P96 a day, the poverty threshold set by government.


The group said that officials should experience firsthand what it is like to make ends meet with the very amount they deem sufficient to keep a Filipino from being classified as poor. “Let them try to cover food, transportation, and other essential needs with just P96 before claiming that it is sufficient for survival,” KMP said.


The group said government’s P14,634 per month threshold is far removed from IBON Foundation estimate that a five-member family requires P1,277 per day to afford a decent standard of living .


KMP cited that food inflation has hit 6.4%, while rice inflation has reached 20.7%, impacting poor families by as much as 9.4 per cent food inflation rate.


“The Filipino masses are forced to tighten their belts, while those in power live in comfort. Our challenge to Marcos and his officials is this: Try living on P96 a day, without dipping into your massive salaries, allowances, and privileges. Let’s see if you can endure the kind of life you impose upon the poor,” said KMP chairperson Danilo Ramos. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Mong Palatino
title: The thrill of group bike rides
content:
Bikers have been bonded by the daily commute or the frequent group rides, and this ritual of biking together can be turned into an advocacy action. This should not be a surprise since the tribe of bikers who regularly ride together suffers from the same grave inefficiencies that plague our roads and communities.

Biking brings calm and exhilaration at the same time, and these feelings are amplified during a group ride.

Planning a group ride takes time and patience, and it is deservedly celebrated when it happens.

It is usually done for leisure, a chill time with fellow bikers. It can be a training session for a scheduled race. Or it can become the power of many if organized to promote a cause.

Whatever the intent that pedals the ride, it is necessary to have trust, coordination, and the unity to move forward in one direction.

Safety measures are learned, relearned, enforced, and adopted during the ride. Newbies take cues from fellow riders, hand signals are introduced, and road rules that apply to cyclists are highlighted in real time. The grounding experience allows bikers to map out routes, rediscover a place from a new perspective, and become familiar with the local scenery. If field trips immerse travelers in history and the tourism value of a town or institution, a group bike tour provides the same allure and they cover even the remote corners that cars and buses cannot reach. A bike tour always offers new ways of seeing and experiencing the peripheries in our communities.

The group ride is an educative activity for all – riders, motorists, commuters, and pedestrians. It makes the bikers more visible, and this is deliberate. A lone biker wishes to be seen for his or her safety, a group ride ensures it and compels the people on the road to acknowledge the space reserved for cyclists. And if a protected bike lane is missing, the bikers crowding the street effectively become the mobile barrier that serves as a reminder not just of the presence of two-wheeled vehicles but also the right of others (non-car drivers) to use the taxpayer-funded road infrastructure.

This is the principle guiding critical mass rides which have become a global movement. An intentional biking of the many to normalize the idea of biking, encourage people to go out and bike, and destigmatize the use of roads by bikers. It is through these collective efforts that a community of bikers is formed. Bikers sharing the joy of biking and pedaling together to remove the perils of the supposedly mundane human act of travelling on a non-motorized vehicle.

There is no single community of bikers, and the diversity of these networks highlights the power that can be harnessed to deliver a message to broader segments in society. Bikers have been bonded by the daily commute or the frequent group rides, and this ritual of biking together can be turned into an advocacy action. This should not be a surprise since the tribe of bikers who regularly ride together suffers from the same grave inefficiencies that plague our roads and communities. They all see, hear, and experience the same daily evils of bad governance that propel citizens to speak out and mobilize.

Imagine a long line of bikers occupying a road, this scene repeated several times until it becomes normal. It is an attempt to rewire our perceptions of what a car-dominated street should look like. Then imagine this determined group of citizens on the move who by their mere presence reveal the glaring inadequacies in urban planning. They can be rallied to challenge car centrism and its morbid manifestations in policymaking, public works, traffic regulations, and toxic road mindset and habits.

The potential of tapping bikers to be active advocates of sociopolitical causes is confirmed by their actual participation in protest actions against controversial issues from the flood corruption scandal in 2025 to Pax Silica this year. Frequent bike rides have been organized to raise public awareness of pressing social concerns such as the critical conditions of rivers, coastal habitats, and watersheds. Both young and old bikers have shown enthusiastic participation in rides that explore historical landmarks and celebrate the opening of parks and green spaces.

Biking alone will not change the world, but it is a brave individual defiance of the norms in our motorized megapolis. Every pedal is a plea for consideration, recognition, and basic kindness. Biking together provides greater visibility and faster …

author: rti_admin
title: Miss X Versus Late Rekha Waghmare: The Selective Outrage of Telangana Civil Society
content:
In Telangana, the term “civil society” evokes images of principled activism: women’s groups marching for justice, human rights organisations amplifying marginalised voices, and political parties channelling public anger into demands for accountability. Yet this activism reveals a troubling selectivity when the victim belongs to a Scheduled Caste (SC) community, especially a vulnerable migrant labourer. The stark contrast between the high-profile handling of the Miss X POCSO case and the alleged gang-rape and murder of Late Rekha Waghmare exposes what can only be described as caste-driven hypocrisy. Telangana’s so-called civil society functions less as a beacon of universal justice and more as a caste society indifferent, even complicit, when atrocities target SC “untouchable” communities.

The Miss X Case: Swift Action, Political Storm, and Current Legal Position

In May 2026, Bandi Sai Bhageerath, son of Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay Kumar, faced serious criminal allegations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The complaint, lodged on May 8, 2026, by the mother of Miss X, a 17-year-old girl, accused him of repeated sexual harassment, assault, emotional manipulation, and coercive acts over several months at various locations, including a farmhouse in Moinabad.

Despite his father’s prominent political standing, the initial state machinery moved with noticeable readiness. Following an intense police manhunt and the issuance of a lookout notice, Telangana police arrested Bhageerath on May 16, 2026. He was remanded to judicial custody, subjected to custodial police interrogation, and the investigation proceeded swiftly amidst massive public scrutiny. Protests erupted across Hyderabad and throughout the state; women’s groups, student organisations, and opposition parties (including BRS, CPI, and others) staged aggressive dharnas and demonstrations demanding accountability and an impartial Special Investigation Team (SIT) probe. The media covered every twist and turn relentlessly, ensuring that political patronage could not quietly bury the case.

Regarding the latest position in the case, after spending over 50 days in judicial detention, Bandi Sai Bhageerath approached the Telangana High Court seeking regular bail. On July 9, 2026, Justice K. Sujana of the Telangana High Court granted him regular bail subject to strict conditions. Following his release on bail, Bhageerath moved the High Court seeking orders to restrain social media platforms and mainstream media outlets from publishing defamatory content or reporting prejudicial material concerning the POCSO case, in which the High Court subsequently passed interim restraining directions and sought counter-affidavits from the respondents. While the prosecution’s trial process and chargesheet proceedings continue under the statutory oversight of the special POCSO court, the case stands out as a prime instance where public mobilisation, political contention, and intense civil society pressure forced law enforcement to register the FIR promptly, arrest a powerful minister’s son, and hold custodial interrogation.

The Late Rekha Waghmare Case: Systemic Silence, Cover-Up, and Institutional Apathy.

At roughly the same time, an appalling horror unfolded in Donkeshwar village, Nandipet Mandal, Nizamabad district. Late Rekha Waghmare, a 32-year-old Scheduled Caste woman and migrant agricultural labourer hailing from Patoda Khurd village in Dharmabad Taluka, Nanded district, Maharashtra, was found dead under highly suspicious circumstances on the afternoon of February 13, 2026.

Since 2021, Rekha and her husband, Devidas Waghmare, along with their two young daughters (Jeevika, aged 10, and Sona, aged 8), had been living in a small shed on the agricultural land of a local influential landlord, Barla Narsing Reddy, working on a salaried labour basis. According to the consistent representations submitted by Rekha’s brother-in-law, Sri S. Sanjeev, the landlord had repeatedly harassed Rekha and attempted to exploit her. On February 13, 2026, Narsing Reddy intentionally sent Devidas away to work at another distant agricultural plot with strict orders not to return until all work was finished. The children were away at school. Taking advantage of Rekha being completely alone, Barla Narsing Reddy and his associate, Vittal Empalwad (or Emphalwar), allegedly broke into the …

author: Önder Algedik
title: Seven things you must never say about COP31
content:
COP31 opened in Antalya on November 9 and its two hosts — Türkiye and Australia — have been busy.

Australia’s Labor government, despite being elected on promises to act for the climate, has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since 2022.

Since September 2025 it has signed 19 fossil fuel agreements: 20-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) contracts, oil and gas exploration pacts with ExxonMobil, Chevron and TotalEnergies, drilling rights from Syria to Somalia, and a deal with Australia’s Woodside.

On top of those come six nuclear and mining agreements, three of them were signed in Seoul on November 3, six days before the summit opened.

One host approves the projects. The other signs the contracts. Together they will run a summit whose Action Agenda does not name coal, oil or gas even once.

Everything is going smoothly. In Türkiye, censorship helps; at least 1270 X accounts were blocked in September alone and, over the past 20 months, trustees have been appointed to 10 television channels.

So, to keep the hosts comfortable, here are seven things you must never talk about.

1. Don’t talk about fossil philanthropy

In June, the foundations of the companies that change Türkiye’s climate the most, including a refinery, car factory, coal power plant, an electricity distributor and even the operator of Antalya airport, set up “Philanthropy for Climate”. They invited environmental groups to the table. The polluters bring the money; civil society brings the legitimacy. Australians who have watched gas companies sponsor festivals and sport will know the model.

2. Don’t talk about the COP31 bill

COP31 is expected to cost close to US$2 billion. When the host agreement came before Türkiye's parliament in July, one party wrote a dissenting opinion and then abstained. Only five MPs voted “No”. An agreement that cost to the public up to US$2 billion bill passed in near silence.

COP31 is, in a sense, a rubbish summit; “Zero waste” heads its list of themes. In August, as rubbish washed up along the Mediterranean coast, the national debate was only about waste imported from Britain. Meanwhile, according to Türkiye’s statistics office, more than 10 million tonnes of waste was burned in 2024. The sky became the landfill.

4. Don't talk about the fossil deals

Has anyone at COP31 mentioned the deals Türkiye signed while preparing to host it? The energy minister posed for photos at every ceremony. A 20-year LNG contract with Mercuria. Exploration in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean with ExxonMobil and TotalEnergies. A global partnership with Chevron, from Iraq to Venezuela. A stake in Kirkuk’s oil fields. Rights to drill in Syria, Libya, Somalia and Pakistan. And Woodside’s LNG.

When I counted in October, there were 14. Now there are 19.

5. Don’t talk about cities without resilience

On October 14, Istanbul, Sakarya, Kocaeli, Yalova, Muğla and Antalya went under water on the same day. The minister of urbanisation, who is also COP31 president, called it a “disaster”, blamed climate change and moved the topic onto the summit’s “Resilient Cities” theme. Were these resilient cities or cities stripped of their resilience? Between 2002 and 2021, Türkiye laid 603 million tonnes of asphalt and poured close to a billion tonnes of cement. If you must, talk only about river beds and pretend the valley slopes above them were never paved. In three days, everyone forgets.

6. Say ‘conference’, not ‘fair’

COP stands for Conference of the Parties. But it has become a Fair of the Parties. The minister announced that 1.5 million visitors are expected! That is not a venue for negotiation; it is an exhibition ground. As I argued last month, the stands will be busy and the products green. Never call it a fair. Say “climate summit”, a phrase with no actor and no action.

Say “coal phase-out”, but never mention oil. Ask for a coal exit date, which buys the government time. Don’t touch the summit’s global business partner, Koç Holding, which owns Türkiye's oil refineries. Call gas a “bridge fuel”. Australians know this one: Labor’s Future Gas Strategy says gas will be needed to 2050 and beyond.

So here are the seven things we must not talk about: Fossil philanthropy, the public bill, a country turned into a dump, fossil deals, asphalt-and-concrete cities, a summit turned trade fair, and oil and gas.

Nobody has to ban any of this, because we already don’t talk about it. We don't talk about the groups that sit at the table with fossil …

author: Odessa Bishop-McMurray
title: “If they won’t give us a future, we will build one right here” - why the French revolt should inspire high-schoolers everywhere
content:
As one of the organisers of the upcoming nationwide 

Students Say No to Hanson

 demonstration on 12 November, I’ve had to endure a lot of inanity from the media and the right. Amongst snide remarks about the stages of brain development and warnings of the mortal dangers of missing two periods of class, one accusation keeps coming up: that we’re plotting to bring “French-style riots” to Australian cities. 

Right-wing journalists seized on an Instagram post we made on 11 October, conveying the inspiration we draw from French student protesters fighting government austerity and the far right. 

Cue an avalanche of hysterical headlines and news segments: The Murdoch-owned Adelaide 

Advertiser

 warned readers to brace for “walkouts ‘inspired’ by violent French protests”. Pauline Hanson went on Brisbane’s 4BC Radio to rip into us:

“...They are saying they are inspired by what’s going on in France. What? The 

looting

? The 

burning

? The 

destruction

? They’re 

inspired

 by that?”

Well, we’re not sorry for being inspired by French students. Everyone who wants to see a better world should identify with their struggle. 

Young people everywhere are facing a dire future, and revolt is rightly spreading. It’s clear even to some in the establishment that what’s happening in France is part of a global wave of protest with deep roots. As former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wrote this week in 

The Guardian

: “A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken—and they know it.”

Both far-right governments and “sensible centrists” are taking us on the same trajectory: more racism, more militarism, and more austerity. 

When states aren’t attempting to re-introduce conscription, as in Germany, they’re funnelling billions into the military-industrial complex while schools crumble. In France, students endure classrooms infested with cockroaches, mould and overcrowding, sometimes numbering 35 students to a class. 

We’ll likely never be able to afford secure housing or sufficient healthcare. We’ve watched politicians choose fossil fuel companies over the habitability of our planet. For many of us, the establishment’s unanimous endorsement of Israel’s genocide in Gaza was the final nail in the coffin.

It’s obvious that the journalists’ and politicians’ pearl-clutching about a few broken Parisian shop windows is a means of avoiding discussion of these issues. And their condemnation of violence rings hollow when they decline to comment on the vastly greater violence that the system inflicts on people daily. 

There’s the violence that is inherent in running such an unequal society. French youth linger without a future in the slums while the richest 500 families own nearly half the country. Schools and hospitals in France are crumbling, but the latest budget announcement includes 54 billion euros in further cuts to public spending. The police systematically brutalise Black and Arab working-class migrants. The high-profile killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, which sparked a nationwide revolt in 2023, is part of a long history of racialised policing. 

When these injustices generate resistance, there’s one public service the government can guarantee: the bludgeoning of protestors, tear gas, and potentially lethal stun grenades; exploding a student’s hand, breaking another’s jaw and leaving two 16-year-olds blinded for life. 

This is an inherent admission that the ruling class has no genuine plan to improve society. They just want resignation from ordinary people, and when that fails, tear gas is their backup plan.

But French students have shown that resignation gets us nowhere; Our power comes from the streets, and that’s a lesson the ruling class desperately does not want students to learn.

Already, France has shown small glimpses of how these movements can win real gains. While still hoping to crush the movement, the government has already been forced to make concessions. They’ve announced plans to cap class sizes, hire more teachers, and create more university places. This is a tiny fraction of what the movement is demanding, but it proves a timeless truth: a month of rebellion can win more change than decades of asking nicely.

A grassroots student movement in Serbia just ended the 14-year rule of the repressive Vučić regime. In Brazil, thousands of students flocked to the streets to successfully halt the advance of far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

It seems like …

author: Beau Lyon
title: Mascot residents organise against hyperscale AI data centre construction
content:
A community group has come together to oppose the Project Duke hyperscale artificial intelligence (AI) data centre planned for Kent Street, Mascot.

Mascot Against AI Datacentres (MAAD) is organising to stop the project, which was approved by the NSW Department of Planning in December last year.

The 90–120 megawatt project was approved under State Significant Development rules that bypass local council approval processes. It would join data centres in nearby Alexandria and Roseberry, including an 18MW data centre on Gardeners Road and an 84MW data centre on Bourke Road.

The processing power required for AI means that these data centres use significantly more energy and water than regular data centres.

Project Duke is the largest approved AI data centre near the CBD. It is set to consume enough energy for 64,000 households and will use as much water a day as 30,000 people. It will also produce constant noise that will impact nearby apartment buildings.

It will feature diesel generators and above ground diesel tanks that can store up to 783,000 liters. While diesel generators are pitched as emergency only reserves, in case of power shortages, some data centres reportedly use diesel generators on a regular basis.

Residents are worried about health impacts from air and noise pollution. “I wouldn’t have bought my home if I knew there was going to be a data centre built here,” said a resident involved in MAAD.

State and federal Labor governments continue to push AI data centres in an effort to make Australia a local hub for the international tech and AI industry, despite concerns that the “AI bubble” might burst.

At least 27 AI data centres are under construction across the country, with more in the planning phase.

Communities are getting organised against AI data centres across the country, and they have already won some back-downs in NSW.

The proposal for an AI data centre on the banks of the Cooks River, in Arncliffe, was defeated by a community-led campaign. Stop Cooking the River said the defeat was a warning to political leaders that local communities will not accept “power and water guzzling AI data centres”.

In Katoomba, a resident noticed a Development Application notice for a 1-2MW data centre in a sensitive nature area. They set up No Data Centre in Katoomba to spread the word and the outcry was so great that the project was scrapped within 17 days.

The controversial 90MW Project Mars AI data centre in Lane Cove was scrapped after a resident-led campaign organised by Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group.

In West Footscray, in Naarm/Melbourne, community group Citizens of Tottenham’s campaign has caused construction delays that have wiped billions off the stock value of data centre giant NextDC.

New opposition groups have formed in Arncliffe, Kemps Creek, Moss Vale and Guildford West, and now in Mascot.

MAAD activist Kyle Barrington said “local residents we spoke to were unaware of the proposal and did not recall receiving the letters that supposedly were sent advising of the plan”.

“No community forums have been held advising of Project Duke or explaining the many negative impacts.”

MAAD is calling for a pause on the construction of Project Duke to engage genuine environment and social impact studies and community consultation. It is joining calls from other community groups for a moratorium on new AI data centres across NSW.

[Sign the Mascot Against AI Datacentres petition here. A statewide rally against AI data centres is being planned for December 5.]

author: Sagar Sanyal
title: Emergency and autocracy in Modi’s India
content:
The far-right government in India led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been increasingly repressive and anti-democratic over recent months. Commentators are asking if the country is in the grip of an ‘

undeclared Emergency

’, a reference to the 1975-77 period of ‘Emergency rule’ by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in which activists and trade unionists were simply rounded up and jailed. 

The current repression is a response to the student and youth protests that erupted in the capital, New Delhi, in late July. They were sparked by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a satirical movement that began on social media a couple of months earlier. The scale and intensity of the protests surprised the regime, as did the mocking anti-Modi tenor of popular chants. While the protest demand was for the resignation of the education minister over exam leaks, the protesters were motivated by visceral opposition to Modi, who has ruled since 2014. The police lashed out using the sort of 

force

 that they typically use in repressed regions like Kashmir. Police fired pellet guns, used nail-studded batons and sexually assaulted women protesters. 

Despite the repression, tens of thousands mobilised daily for five days—high school and university students, middle-class and working-class youth. Not only in Delhi, but in dozens of cities around the country. Alongside clips of police brutality circulating on social media, there are clips of youth chasing police off the streets with their sheer numbers and bravado. There are clips of cheeky middle-class youth approaching police who are away from the heat of the action to ask mocking questions like “Dear Mr. Officer, are you planning to tear gas protesters today?” The government is tracking down incriminating and embarrassing recordings of those events and asking social media platforms to 

remove them

.

Public opinion has turned strongly against Modi’s repression. Among the Hindi-speaking, middle-class, upper-caste Hindus who have been the most secure vote base of the BJP, parents now saw their own children being beaten—just for demanding a fair opportunity in college exams! Ultimately, the administration conceded the protest demand to sack the education minister, a humiliating 

defeat

 for Modi. It gave the lie to the “unstoppable strongman” image of him so carefully crafted by pro-Modi big media. 

Less than three months after the July protests, a new protest movement gripped the nation. It demands the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Gyanesh Kumar, who has been highly partisan to Modi and his 

Hindu nationalist

 Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and, according to some parties, rigged state elections in Bihar (May 2025) and West Bengal (April 2026). In West Bengal, the BJP won for the first time due in part to the chief election commissioner disqualifying millions of names from the eligible voters list. Deletions disproportionately targeted Muslims, who are an ideological enemy of Hindu nationalists, and who were also an important vote base of the party the BJP displaced—the Trinamool Congress (TMC). 

Following a late September 

expose,

 which revealed that the chief election commissioner had overruled the protestations of even his fellow election commissioners, the CJP and left student groups took up vote-rigging as a national campaign to channel the energy from the July student movement. Demands for the chief election commissioner to resign have been taken up by all opponents of the BJP. 

When a large protest was called for 

10 October

, the state responded by locking down New Delhi. Around 40,000 paramilitary and police laid siege to a sizeable area around the “designated protest site” of Jantar Mantar in the centre of the city. They blocked roads and shut down local internet mobile services (India is 

among the worst

 states for this). They closed over 40 metro train stations in Delhi and stopped over 200 inter-city trains from reaching Delhi. They threatened activists in their homes on the night before the march, this coming on top of regular arbitrary detention of prominent leaders of the protest movement (from the CJP and the left parties). 

Undeterred

, protestors appeared in their tens of thousands and were again met with batons and tear gas, and thousands were detained.

Sizeable protests have continued sporadically since 10 October, some called by the CJP or student organizations of the left, 

others

 by major opposition parties. The …

author: Richard Boult
title: NSW Police take Rising Tide to Supreme Court over Newcastle Harbour paddle out protest
content:
New South Wales Police are once again attempting to stop a climate protest in Muloobinba/Newcastle from going ahead.

It announced on November 6 that it would take Rising Tide (RT) to the Supreme Court to try and stop the Paddle for the Planet protest on November 14.

Hundreds are set to join the paddle out into Newcastle Harbour — the world’s largest coal port — on kayaks, canoes, surfboards and other watercraft. Thousands more will support from the shore.

NSW Police has taken RT to court for previous protests in Newcastle Harbour, and have carried out mass arrests of protesters, most of whom have had their charges dropped.

NSW Police are challenging the event’s Form 1, or Notice of Intention to Hold a Public Assembly, which gives protesters legal protection against obstruction charges and move-on orders.

RT said the paddle out will go ahead regardless of the Supreme Court’s decision.

“We have a legal right to assemble and a right to protest without permission, and it’s legal to gather in public places and to paddle in the Newcastle Harbour,” it said.

“Police cannot outlaw protest … We have a great legal team from Climate Defenders Australia who will be arguing our case in the Supreme Court and we’re feeling hopeful about our prospects.

“But regardless of the court outcome, Paddle for the Planet will still go ahead.”

The protest coincides with the United Nations COP31 climate conference and aims to highlight the hypocrisy of federal Labor claiming to address climate change while approving new coal and gas projects.

“We’re already feeling the devastating impacts of the climate crisis; many thousands of lives have been lost in recent months across the Asian continent, in flash and monsoonal floods and heatwaves, and scientists project that almost half a million people around the world will die by February due to the climate-fueled super El Niño,” RT said.

NSW Labor police minister Yasmin Catley said she “backs” the police decision to try and stop the protest, citing safety concerns.

“The only safety issue here is the Labor government's reckless expansion of coal and gas fuelling dangerous climate change,” RT said.

Steve O’Brien, Socialist Alliance candidate for Newcastle, said Labor thinks approving coal mines and blocking protests could shore up its vote in the Hunter region.

“This will not address years of Labor’s neglect … the Mater hospital, for example, is a mould infested mess, buses remain privatised and it’s a long wait at the Adamstown crossing when the coal wagons roll by.

“Rising Tide is spot on to point out the need to protect the right to protest. NSW Premier Chris Minns would rather silence dissent than take real action on climate change.”

[Join the Paddle for the Planet on November 14.]

author: Rick Kuhn
title: Unemployment: a feature of capitalism, not a bug
content:
Today more than one in ten workers can’t find enough paid labour to live a decent life. And that’s only workers actively looking for a job or for more hours of employment. It doesn’t count those who have given up on finding a job, even though they want one, and survive thanks to friends, family or a measly government payment that isn’t an unemployment benefit.

In September

 the seasonally adjusted

un

employment rate was 4.7 percent;

under

employment was 6.3 percent. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, you’re not unemployed if you worked even an hour in the survey fortnight.

To get the Jobseeker Payment or Youth Allowance the un- and underemployed have to follow the Albanese government’s savage eligibility rules, inherited from its Liberal predecessors. If you earn more than a pitiful $75 a week, your payment starts to go down. You must follow the instructions of Workforce Australia and, if you’ve been directed to one, of an outsourced “employment services provider” agency, which profits from government funding.

That may mean applying for a certain number of jobs every “reporting period”, doing training they tell you to do, however meaningless courses about writing job applications or behaviour during an interview might be; or perform “work for the dole”, that would normally be done for much higher award wages. You have to “accept any offer of suitable paid work”, defined by the provider, whether the type of work or its location actually suits you or not.

If you’re single, without kids, the dole is

currently


a princely $413 a week. Certainly in Sydney, you’d be very lucky if less than half of that went on renting a room. And if you’re young, that’s unfortunate: unemployed aged 21 or younger are penalised and get less money than those over 21. Apparently young people don’t need as much shelter, food, clothing, etc. as older people.

Both the unemployment and underemployment rates are rising.

Unemployment is not a bug in capitalism, but a feature. The threat of un- and underemployment – descending into what Marx called “

the industrial reserve army

”—disciplines workers fearful of losing their jobs. The higher the level of unemployment, other things being equal, the less likely they are to take risks by fighting to defend or improve their pay and conditions.

The extent of the reserve army of labour changes in the course of economic cycles: lower during booms, higher in slumps.

Many central banks, like the Reserve Bank of Australia, are bumping up interest rates to slow their countries’ economies down. Their goal is not increased unemployment; that’s a side effect. Their main target is the rate of inflation. High inflation—lack of stability in the purchasing power of money—makes calculations by capitalists about their activities and especially investments more difficult.

In legislation

, the RBA has two goals: “price stability and the maintenance of full employment”. It says that “

[t]hese two objectives usually work together

”. In practice, the bank favours sacrificing jobs to keep a lid on inflation.

But today, high oil prices, due to the USA’s and Israel’s war on Iran, is the main driver of inflation. The RBA isn’t bumping up interest rates to discipline workers, although that’s a side-effect. Governor

Michelle Bullock

said at the end of September that “There is no wage price spiral going on in Australia. Rises in wages are not driving … cost pressures”.

In fact, it is workers who are mainly affected by inflation. Greg Jericho, in the

Guardian

, has illustrated how workers’ real pay has been falling since 2021, compared with the Consumer Price Index by 7 percent; compared with the more appropriate Employee Living Cost Index, by more than 12 percent.

The hostility of most union officials to leading their members in serious struggles to defend, let alone restore or improve their living standards, is mainly to blame.

In his 1972 report

Poverty in Australia

, Ronald Henderson, appointed by the Liberal government of Billy McMahon, calculated a poverty line, marking an “austere” standard of living below which people were in poverty. The Melbourne Institute of Economic Research frequently updates it.

JobSeeker

has consistently been below this line. Today that unemployment benefit is less than half the

Henderson poverty line

. Using 50, let alone 60 percent of median

household income

, common alternative international measures of poverty, the situation of people on JobSeeker …

author: Priya T.
title: Workers can overthrow capitalism
content:
Human beings are the most cooperative species that have ever existed. The expectation that we will live socially, with other people to help and guide us, is built into our biology. 

Compare a human baby with, say, crocodiles, which are born with as many as 60 teeth and use them to break through their eggshell, fending for themselves from their earliest moments. Or baby horses, who can walk within an hour of birth. Human babies can’t so much as lift their own heads

.

Our evolutionary survival instinct is to

cry

, the single purpose of which is to

alert others

 to needs or distress. This interdependence continues, in various ways, throughout our lives.

The fact that humans are not designed to make it alone is why capitalism feels so deeply wrong to so many of us. It is not geared towards meeting people’s needs, and the values it promotes—individualism, competition and greed—run counter to the social and collective instincts that are crucial to our survival as a species. 

The enormous resources and technologies that capitalism brings into existence are not used to provide for people or distributed to meet need. Instead, they are bought and sold to generate wealth for the tiny minority who control them. This gap between how things are, and how they could and should be, is one of the features of the system that perpetually cause people to turn against it. And it is becoming increasingly obscene. 

At the same time as the super-rich are getting on commercial space flights—at $70 million a ticket—the majority of the world’s population have never set foot on a plane. While the ultra-wealthy pour resources into the pursuit of immortality

for themselves,

wasting millions on cryogenic chambers, organ replacement, blood transfusions and uploading themselves to the cloud, millions of children die from diarrhea-related illnesses every year, and 3.4 billion people live without proper sanitation. Twelve billionaires hold more wealth than half of humanity. Abundance exists, but it is hoarded away from the masses. 

The rich would like us to think they earned and therefore deserve this wealth; that they are compensated in proportion to what they contribute to society. Australia’s richest person Gina Rinehart wrote a column expressing this view for the industry publication

Australian Resources and Investment

in 2012: “If you’re jealous of those with more money, don’t just sit there and complain; do something to make more money yourself—spend less time drinking, or smoking, or socialising, and more time working.” 

Leaving aside that Rinehart seems to spend heaps of time drinking and socialising, including at expensive Italian hotels with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, nobody really thinks that a mining executive works harder than a garbage truck driver or early childhood educator. But the reality is that on average Australian salaries, it would take these workers about 650,000 years of “more time working” to earn the $40 billion Rinehart is worth. 

The truth is that the ruling class amasses their wealth not by working harder than everyone else, but by getting

other people to work for them

. Wealth is “created” when the value of the products other people produce is greater than what they are paid by their bosses in wages. This is called exploitation, and it is the basis of capital accumulation. 

Without the labour of workers, bosses wouldn’t have profits or power. Workers do the work to produce what we all need, while the “work” bosses do is to protect their control over this process, make it more profitable and manage the profits. This control gives bosses the ability to shape the lives of millions if not billions of other people—they decide what is made, who gets it and what it sells for. 

The majority, on the other hand, are oppressed: they are denied control over their own activity, as well as what happens to the products of their labour and, by extension, how their society is organised. This oppression is a prerequisite for exploitation—workers are conditioned from birth into accepting their subordinate place in society, and are expected to accept it throughout their working lives. Whether this is unadulterated, as in tyrannical dictatorships, or sanitised, as in parliamentary democracies, the underlying reality is the same. Bosses exercise dictatorial authority in the workplace. And their interests inform government policy. 

The majority of us get little to no say over what happens in our communities …

author: Kerry Smith
title: Community campaign forces Westpac to end Palantir contract
content:
Two months after Coles announced it would cut ties with surveillance company Palantir, Westpac has announced it will not renew its contract with the company, bending to a powerful community campaign

More than 40 organisations have joined the Dump Palantir Coalition (DPC) to pressure organisations to end contracts with the technology company over its role in supplying Israel’s genocide in Gaza and United States President Donald Trump’s deportation regime.

Palantir, founded by tech billionaire Peter Thiel, signed a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defense in January 2024, to supply technology and surveillance to support its genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank.

United Nations Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese named Palantir as being among those companies profiting from an “economy of genocide”.

Palantir supplied a US$30 million system to support Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) identification, tracking and deportation of migrants.

DPC spokesperson Mustafa Saabi said a “global movement” is determined to drive Palantir out of businesses, governments and institutions.

“When a protester told Palantir CEO Alex Karp that his company’s technology kills Palestinians, he replied: ‘Mostly terrorists. That’s true.’

“The UN has found that nearly 70% of the deaths it verified in Gaza were women and children … That’s the company Westpac was doing business with.

“This isn’t a public relations problem Palantir can fix with better messaging.”

The day Westpac reported its decision, Palantir shares fell by 7.3%, temporarily wiping about US$32 billion from its market value.

Westpac’s claim that its decision to end the contract with Palantir came down to “technology simplification” ignores the powerful public pressure campaign.

“Westpac didn’t wake up with a conscience,” Justice for Palestine Magan-djin spokesperson Remah Naji said. “We made its relationship with Palantir a liability. “"GetUp and SIX mobilised thousands of consumers and shareholders. Grassroots Palestine groups organised across the country. Ordinary people stood up, and we won.

"First Coles. Now Westpac. Every company doing business with Palantir should be asking itself one question: are we next?"

DPC spokesperson Subhi Awad said public money is still flowing to Palantir through the Future Fund, which holds $114.6 million in Palantir shares and government agencies continue to purchase Palantir technology.

“We’re coming for those relationships too,” Awad said. “Our message is simple: do business with Palantir and you risk losing customers and wrecking your reputation.

“We organised. We made Westpac dump them. And we’re not finished.”

[Sign up for updates about the next Dump Palantir Coalition campaign.]

Justice for Palestine Magan-djin

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Victorian Liberals flag free speech crackdown
content:
State Liberal leader Jess Wilson has used a book launch to make public her intent to ban protests and political phrases in Victoria if elected in November. 

Speaking

 in Caulfield at the launch of 

Bondi Terror

, written by a SkyNews host and Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive officer Alex Ryvchin, Wilson 

linked

 the movement for Palestine with the horrific violence in Bondi. “When governments, both at federal and state levels, allow hatred like ‘all Zionists are terrorists’, and ‘globalise the intifada’ to be spewed and normalised on our streets, at our universities, and online—Bondi is the result” she said. 

There is still no evidence that the Bondi shooters had ever attended a pro-Palestine protest or otherwise been part of the movement against Israel’s genocide, nor that they had set foot on a university campus or championed the slogan “globalise the intifada”. 

Nevertheless, Wilson told the crowd “Under my leadership, we will expand bans on speech that amounts to incitement to violence, like “Globalise the Intifada”. She also announced her intention to introduce move on laws and to require protests gain permits, so that “all Victorians can feel safe in the city they love”. Except presumably those wanting to exercise the democratic right to protest or use slogans that the government objects to. 

These measures have been demanded by sections of the business and the political right in Melbourne for some time. During the most acute phase of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, when weekly protests took place in Melbourne’s CBD, much anger was expressed at the supposed disruption to normal trade. Melbourne city mayor Nick Reece 

claimed

 he received “weekly phone calls from restaurateurs and city retailers telling me the protests are having a real, negative impact on their business”, particularly “Sunday yum cha”. Never mind there was not one documented case of a Palestine protester preventing someone having yum cha, even imaginary threats to small business bottom lines trump a genocide in the world of council and right-wing politics.  

Last year Brad Battin, the leader of the Liberals at the time, announced the Liberals would introduce a 

permit system

, following the Melbourne City council approval of a plan to request state and federal governments to restrict protest rights. Wilson has now recommitted the Liberals to this plan. 

Wilson and the Victorian Liberals are only the latest to get on the anti-free speech bandwagon. The Liberal Nation Party government in Queensland has already criminalised the phrases “From the river to the sea” and “Globalise the intifada”. Dozens of activists have been charged and are facing jail time because of these laws. An appeal to the High Court against the laws has been launched by pro-Palestine activists, based on the implied right to political communication in the Constitution. In October, the New South Wales Labor government 

joined

 the case on the side of the Queensland government, defending the Orwellian laws. This comes after Minns’ anti-protest laws were 

struck down

 as unconstitutional by the New South Wales Supreme Court. 

There is no sign of this offensive abating. Antisemitism envoy Jillian Segal in October released a 

report

 calling for exclusion zones for protests and bans on face coverings, explicitly declaring “progressive” antisemitism to be the “most pervasive” form of antisemitism. Segal is increasingly open about her purpose being to reframe opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza and support for the liberation of Palestinians as racism towards Jewish people and therefore unacceptable and unlawful. 

If the Victorian Liberals win in November, as is now looking 

increasingly likely

, we will have to launch vigorous campaigns to defend our rights to freedom of speech and the right to assembly.

author: Unknown
title: Kayyım gölgesinde belediye sözleşmeleri: İşçiler nasıl seyirciye çevrildi?
content:
Genel İşler iş kolunda yerel hizmetleri ve belediyeleri kapsayan sözleşmeler sırayla imzalanırken, sözleşmelerin seyrine ve işçiler arasında öne çıkan eğilimlere dair birkaç not düşmenin önümüzdeki tartışmalar açısından önemli olacağını düşünüyoruz. İBB’de peş peşe imzalanan ve zam oranları gerçekte yüzde 20’yi aşmayan sözleşmelerin ardından sırasıyla Ataşehir, Kartal ve Maltepe belediyelerinde de sözleşmeler imzalandı. Sırada Kadıköy sözleşmesi var. Bu notları iki yazıda ele alacağız.

Geçen sözleşme döneminde, başta Kartal Belediyesi dış şantiyesi olmak üzere belediye işçileri imzalanan zam oranlarına karşı lokal iş durdurmalar yapmıştı; ancak bu karşı çıkış yenilgiyle sonuçlanmıştı. Belediye yönetimlerinin baskısına, sendika genel merkezlerinin işçiye sormadan, şubelerin inisiyatifini ellerinden alarak sözleşmeleri üstten imzalamasına dair geçmiş deneyimler eklendi; bu tutumun şubeler üzerinde yarattığı baskı ve şube yönetimlerinin ortak tutum almaktan kaçınması bu sonuçta belirleyici oldu. İşçilerin bu karşı çıkışını ve ortak hareket etmek için gösterdikleri inisiyatifi bir kazanım olarak hanemize yazsak da bu deneyimden olumlu sonuçlar çıkarmaları engellendi. Birçok işçinin dile getirdiği “İş durduruyoruz, kaybeden biz oluyoruz, yevmiyemiz kesiliyor, grev bittikten sonra daha çok çöp topluyoruz” serzenişinin altında biraz da sonuçsuz kalan bu eylemler yattı. Grevlerin ortasında işçinin beklentilerine yanıt vermeden imzalanan sözleşmeler, işçiler arasında “Biz greve çıkıyoruz, 3. gün aniden imzalanıyor, biz niye 3 gün yevmiyemizden oluyoruz?” gibi sözlere zemin hazırladı. İşçilerin bu grev ve iş durdurmalardan neler kazandığına ayrıca bir parantez açmak gerekiyor; ama önce, sürekli yarıda kalan bu mücadelelerin işçileri TİS süreçlerinde izleyici konumuna ittiğini söyleyebiliriz. “Zaten ne kazanacağımızı belirleyemiyoruz, şube ne alabiliyorsa alsın işte” düşüncesi hakim eğilimlerden biri oldu.

İzmir’de belediye işçilerinin hedef gösterilmesiyle örgütlenen linç kampanyası, işçilerin birbirini izleyen eylemleri sayesinde onları kolayca teslim alamadı. Ama bu süreçte işçileri tehdit eden, onları bir gider kalemi olarak gösterip halka şikayet eden, belediyelerde gerçekleştiremedikleri her şeyi işçilerin sırtına yıkan ve belediye işçilerinin ücretlerinin neden açlık sınırının üzerinde olduğunu tartıştıran bir anlayışla, Saray rejiminin sermaye programına bağlanan bir ucuz iş gücü rejimi uygulandı. AKP’nin kayyım saldırısının yarattığı iş güvencesizliği ortamını kendi saldırılarına dayanak yapan belediyeler, beğenmeyene kapıyı göstermekte ve kayyım sopasını işaret etmekte cesaretlendi. Ayrıca kayyım tehlikesinin halkta belediyeleri sahiplenme duygusu yarattığını bilen belediye yönetimleri, mağduru oynayarak işçilerin sözleşmelerini süzgece çevirdi. Bizi takip eden okurlarımız, 2025 sonu ile 2026 başında onlarca belediyede aynı anda ücretlerin geciktirildiğini, maaş ve mesailerin ödenmediğini, işçilere ne zaman ödeneceğine dair bir açıklama bile yapılmadığını hatırlayacaktır. Ödemeler yapıldığında ise işçilerin deyimiyle para “pul” olmuştu: Geriye dönük alacaklar, ödenmesi gereken tarihten neredeyse 8-9 ay sonra taksitlerle ödendi ve enflasyon marifetiyle eritildi. Henüz kayyım gelmemiş ama “Kayyım yönetse böyle yönetirdi” dediğimiz belediyeler bir yandan sosyal belediyecilik rüzgarları estirdi, öte yandan en çarpıcı örneği İzmir’de görüldüğü gibi on binlerce işçinin ekmeğiyle oynadı, işçileri havuz sisteminde boğmaya kalktı. İşte işçiler, sözleşmelerindeki ücretlerin bile ödenmediği bu koşullarda yeni TİS’ten daha az umutlu hale geldi.

Bu umutsuzluğun bir ayağı da sendikacılar. Belediye işçileri, geçmiş sözleşme dönemlerinde Hizmet-İş, Belediye-İş ve Genel-İş’ten bekledikleri desteği ve önderliği göremedi. Yine lokal diyebileceğimiz bazı belediyelerde Genel-İş’e bağlı kimi şubeler ya da şubelerden bağımsız tutum alan bazı temsilciler ve işçi grupları bu eylemlere önderlik etmeye, en azından önlerini kesmemeye çalıştı. Ama genel olarak “Sendikamız bizim arkamızda durmaz” eğiliminin son 3 sözleşme döneminde (6 yıl) güçlendiği, işçilerin üzerinde uzlaştığı bir tespittir.

Bilindiği gibi AKP’li belediyeler hem ücret politikasında hem de sosyal haklarda CHP’li ve Yeni Partili belediyelerin gerisinde. İşçilerin örgütlenmemesi için de her yolu deniyorlar. Ancak aynı tutum, başka söylemlerle CHP’li, şimdilerde Yeni Partili belediyelerde de var; üstelik buralarda işçiler daha örgütlü olduğu için daha hızlı açığa çıkıyor …

author: CNT Madrid
title: 8 razones para parar en el sector de la prensa y la comunicación este 11-N
content:
Si trabajas en medios de comunicación escritos, en línea o en papel, en radios, en teles o en agencias de publicidad, diseño o cualquier ámbito de la comunicación te sobran los motivos para ir a la huelga este miércoles 11 de noviembre. Aquí la sección de trabajadoras de la Prensa y la Comunicación de la CNT de Madrid y la CGT y las trabajadoras en el sector de la comunicación del Sindicato de Artes Gráficas, Papel, Comunicación y Espectáculos de CGT Mad-Castilla-La Mancha-Ext te dan, al menos, ocho motivos más:


SALARIOS QUE CIERREN LAS HERIDAS ABIERTAS DESDE 2008 Y QUE ALIVIEN LA CRISIS DE ASEQUIBILIDAD DE LA VIDA Y LA VIVIENDA


Tras más de quince años de ERE, despidos y congelaciones, la profesión sigue sin recuperarse, agravando el encarecimiento general de la vida y, en concreto, los problemas para acceder a una vivienda digna que sufre toda la clase trabajadora. Entre los periodistas con contrato, cerca de la mitad cobra entre 1.000 y 2.000 euros netos al mes. Entre los autónomos, algo más de la mitad recibe menos de 100 euros por pieza. Exigimos subidas salariales que devuelvan el poder adquisitivo perdido y salarios mínimos del sector a la altura de la responsabilidad del oficio.


CONVENIOS VIVOS, NO CONVENIOS CADUCADOS


La patronal deja morir los convenios sectoriales, empezando por el de Prensa Diaria. Exigimos su renovación y actualización inmediata con tablas salariales al día. Exigimos también que se cumpla la obligatoriedad de los planes de igualdad en las empresas informativas.


REDACCIONES SIN BRECHAS


Las mujeres son mayoría en las redacciones, pero sólo 19 de los 100 medios con más audiencia de España estaban dirigidos por una mujer en 2025, dos menos que en 2024. Exigimos acabar con la brecha de género en salarios y ascensos. Exigimos reducir la distancia entre direcciones y jefaturas, de un lado, y redactoras, redactores, productoras, productores y personal técnico, del otro, que son quienes sostienen el día a día.


CADA HORA, REGISTRADA Y PAGADA


La actualidad no entiende de horarios, pero eso no puede ser excusa para el trabajo gratis. La mayoría de los periodistas trabaja más de 40 horas semanales, el máximo legal del Estatuto de los Trabajadore. Muchas veces trabajan más de 45 y de 50 horas… Exigimos un registro real de jornada y el reconocimiento de las horas extraordinarias, compensadas en dinero o en descanso. La dedicación especial que exige este oficio no puede salir gratis a las empresas.


INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL AL SERVICIO DE LA INFORMACIÓN, NO CONTRA QUIENES LA HACEN


Exigimos que el uso de la IA se negocie y se regule en los convenios. No aceptaremos que la automatización sirva para sustituir a profesionales ni para recortar plantillas. Cada puesto que se pierde así degrada la calidad informativa y pone en riesgo el derecho de la ciudadanía a una información veraz.


SEGURIDAD FÍSICA Y ECONÓMICA GARANTIZADA POR CONVENIO


Exigimos que quien cubre conflictos, catástrofes, manifestaciones o cualquier información de riesgo tenga por convenio seguros, protocolos de protección, material adecuado y respaldo económico y jurídico. Esas garantías deben valer también para freelances y colaboradores, no solo para la plantilla.


TELETRABAJO Y CONCILIACIÓN COMO MODELO NATURAL DEL SECTOR


El periodismo ya se hace desde cualquier lugar. Exigimos que el teletrabajo y la jornada sean compatibles con el descanso y el cuidado de nuestros familiares. Y que sean un derecho regulado y compensado en los convenios, y no una concesión que la empresa da y quita a voluntad. Los gastos deben ir a cargo de la empresa y el derecho a la desconexión digital debe estar garantizado.


CONTRA LA PRECARIEDAD Y POR LA ESTABILIDAD EN EL EMPLEO


Que las becas no sustituyan puestos de trabajo: tener becarios es una práctica habitual en nuestro sector y su figura se ha convertido en caldo de cultivo para tener trabajadores y trabajadoras a bajo coste y de las que se pueda prescindir libremente. Algo similar ocurre con los falsos autónomos, personas obligadas a darse de alta como autónomo pero que en realidad dependen completamente de la empresa como cualquier otra en plantilla. Exigimos la desaparición del fraude y el respeto a la legalidad en el empleo.


La entrada

8 razones para parar en el sector de la prensa y la comunicación este 11-N

 se publicó primero en

Sindicato CNT de Madrid

.

author: Ashley Smith
title: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle
content:
We must develop new modes of organizing that go beyond a narrow focus on labor law and shop floor issues.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A political and economic battle against today’s robber barons — the billionaire and trillionaire class of tech bosses — is unfolding on many fronts as tech workers agitate against these oligarchs’ complicity with the U.S. military, the cops, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Israeli occupation of Palestine.

In their new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry, JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine recount the emergence of the tech workers’ movement over the last two decades, from the political campaigns they have launched to the heroic strikes they have staged against companies like Kickstarter and The New York Times.

No armchair analysts, Tan and Redwine are tech worker leaders who have been at the heart of many of these fights. In this interview, they discuss the rise of the movement, the workers’ turn to unionization, and the oligarchs’ adoption of authoritarianism and austerity to crush it. And they draw lessons from this struggle not only for tech workers, but for the entire labor movement.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Ashley Smith: The tech workers’ movement was first spurred into action by the radicalization and social movements triggered by the Great Recession. Workers launched campaigns against their companies’ contracts with, for instance, the U.S. military and ICE. What strategies and tactics did workers use?

JS Tan: After the Great Recession, corporate America thought the tech sector was going to rejuvenate the U.S. economy. The tech bosses were aligned with the Democratic Party and embraced things like identity politics and put forth a progressive, democratic vision of the future.

But the industry’s workers realized that the tech sector was not living up to its mission statements and public pronouncements. They were making software for the U.S. military, ICE, and police. And their internal culture was rife with sexism and racism.

So, tech workers launched campaigns to expose their bosses’ hypocrisy. A good example of this is the Google workers’ campaign against the company’s Project Maven, which used AI to analyze military drone footage.

Workers mobilized their radical co-workers and went public with an open letter [to Google CEO Sundar Pichai] in The New York Times. That exposure forced the company to concede to their demand not to renew its Project Maven contract. Simplifying greatly, the tech movement as a whole adopted this strategy of mobilization behind open letters.

This provoked opposition from the tech oligarchy. It abandoned its California liberalism, which included opposition to Donald Trump in his first term, and instead largely backed him in his second term. What caused this political reorientation? How did it change their companies and treatment of workers?

Tan: In our book, we show how the battle in the tech industry led both workers and bosses to acquire class consciousness. It was a process of radicalization on both sides. Initially, the bosses expressed sympathy with the upsurge of tech worker activism, conceded to their workers’ demands, and implemented DEI [diversity, equity, and inclusion] initiatives.

But they got fed up with being told how to run their businesses and started retaliating against their workers for writing open letters, participating in walkouts, and starting union drives. Then, after the pandemic, the Federal Reserve Bank ended its zero-interest rate policy to combat the sharp rise in inflation.

Suddenly, the tech companies lost access to cheap credit and lost billions of dollars in market valuation. To restore their profit margins, they enacted mass layoffs (being asset-light businesses, employee salaries were their largest costs), return-to-work orders, and speed-ups of the remaining workforce.

Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter is a paradigmatic example. He fired 80 percent of the workforce. He combined that with an ideological assault on the company, targeting teams that oversaw human rights, AI ethics, and content moderation — the teams he believed housed the most progressive, pro-union workers. Seeing this, other tech bosses followed suit, imposing a new normal of authoritarianism, austerity, and …

author: anred
title: Falta de recursos y medicación para la salud mental
content:
El jueves  por la mañana los trabajadores de Salud Mental del Hospital Evita realizaron una asamblea. Con la participación de trabajadores, residentes, Farmacia, usuarios, familiares, organizaciones sociales, docentes y estudiantes, denunciaron la falta de recursos para atender la creciente demanda de atención y de medicación. 

Red Eco Alternativo – ANRed 


(Red Eco-Anred) Buenos Aires – “Nos convocó la preocupación por la falta de medicación y por las condiciones en las que venimos atendiendo, con una demanda que sigue creciendo y recursos que no acompañan ese aumento”, subrayan los trabajadores en un comunicado.


Los trabajadores expresaron que se dificulta cada vez más sostener los tratamientos y que en los últimos meses vienen llevando adelante mecanismos para sostener la medicación que necesitan los pacientes. En este sentido, ponen los ejemplos de pedir remedios a otros hospitales, modificar esquemas y entregar recetas para que los pacientes puedan comprarlos. El quiebre se produce, señalan en el documento, porque “llegamos a un punto en el que esas opciones ya no alcanzan. Muchos no tienen cómo pagar los medicamentos y la falta de continuidad termina afectando su salud, con descompensaciones y nuevas consultas a la guardia”.


Los trabajadores del sector de Farmacia explicaron las dificultades que generaron los cambios en el financiamiento y las compras. Si bien, contaron, se había conseguido una provisión excepcional del Ministerio de Salud para cubrir buena parte de las necesidades de noviembre, al momento de la asamblea todavía no había llegado. También comentaron que hay gestiones para diciembre y una planificación para el año próximo. Los trabajadores insistieron que necesitan una provisión sostenida, porque no pueden seguir resolviendo los tratamientos mes a mes sin saber con qué van a contar.


Subrayaron el desborde de la atención por guardia y detallaron que ese desborde se traduce en lo cotidiano en pacientes que permanecen en sillas o camillas en los pasillos y en las dificultades para atender con privacidad y en condiciones adecuadas. Se señalaron problemas de higiene, de espacio y de equipamiento.


El equipo de Salud Mental tampoco tiene un lugar propio donde reunirse, discutir las situaciones y registrar lo trabajado. Muchas veces terminan buscando un espacio prestado en otros servicios. También se destacó cuánto sostienen los residentes la atención diaria y las condiciones en las que se están formando y trabajando.


Otra preocupación fue la atención de niños y adolescentes. Se planteó que la demanda viene aumentando y que faltan recursos específicos para dar respuesta. Los adolescentes de entre 15 y 18 años quedan en la guardia junto con adultos, sin un espacio acorde con sus necesidades. En este sentido, los trabajadores enfatizaron en exigir una respuesta institucional y regional que permita alojarlos y cuidarlos de una manera más adecuada.


La denuncia que realizaron en esta asamblea también se extendió hasta la imposibilidad de conseguir turnos tras la atención por guardia. Expresaron en el documento que después de la guardia “conseguir turnos para continuar un tratamiento en el lugar donde vive cada paciente se vuelve muy difícil. El consultorio de posguardia, que se pensó como un acompañamiento de unos dos meses, termina siguiendo pacientes durante seis meses o más porque no se consigue dónde derivarlos”. Se mencionaron, además, “las dificultades de otros dispositivos, como la UPA, y la necesidad de contar con equipos completos y alternativas que permitan sostener los cuidados fuera de la guardia”.


A esta situación se suma que los pacientes provienen de contextos de mayor vulnerabilidad social, con problemas de vivienda, endeudamiento, desempleo y consumos problemáticos. “Poner el cuerpo y sostener la atención con el esfuerzo de los equipos, tiene un límite”, explicaron.


Finalmente, los trabajadores junto a la comunidad y organizaciones acompañantes decidieron reunirse con los trabajadores del Hospital Esteves para aunar problemáticas, elaborar un petitorio con los problemas y reclamos planteados, ampliar la convocatoria a otros servicios, centros de salud y espacios de la comunidad y la convocatoria a una nueva asamblea para el 19 de noviembre.

author: Unknown
title: Fransa’daki isyanın anatomisi
content:
Kısa zamanda tüm Fransa’ya yayılan öğrenci eylemlerinin ilk tohumu 17 Eylül’de Créteil’deki Saint-Exupéry Lisesi’nde atıldı. Küçük bir grup lise son sınıf öğrencisi akşam üstü saatlerinde, eğitimci eksikliği nedeniyle grev yapan öğretmenlerini desteklemeye karar verdi.


Kendi deyimleriyle anlık gelişen bu kararı “

yarın biz de şansımızı deneyelim, sesimizi duyuralım ve bir şeyleri değiştirmeye çalışalım

” fikri izledi. Ertesi sabah birkaç çöp kutusu ve tel örgüyle ilk barikatı kurdular. Saint-Exupéry öğrencilerini eyleme geçiren temel mesele fırsat eşitliğiydi:


“Kırıp dökmek için değil, haklarımızı talep etmek için buradayız. İmkansızı istemiyoruz. Aslında asgari düzeyde bir şey istiyoruz: Eşitlik. Banliyö ile örneğin 16. bölge arasında eşitlik, başarı için fırsat eşitliği.” 


21 Eylül’deki ablukaya LFI (Boyun Eğmeyen Fransa) partisinden iki milletvekilinin katılması, haberin medyada yer bulması protestoların yaygınlaşmasında etkili oldu. 24 Eylül’e gelindiğinde eylem yapılan okulların sayısı Paris’i de kapsayan Île de France bölgesinde 10’u aşmıştı. Gerekçeler yine benzerdi. Seine-Saint-Denis’de bulunan Saint-Ouen okulundan 14 yaşındaki Abdelaziz’in söylediği gibi:


“Biz biraz yoksul bir liseyiz. Pazartesi ve salı saat 8’den akşam altıya kadar ders var. Sınıfta 34 öğrenciyiz, bazen boş sandalye, masa bile bulamıyoruz. Diğer liselerdeki ablukanın işe yaradığını gördük ve eylem organize etmek için biz de bir Snap grubu oluşturduk...”


İlk eylemlere sahne olan Créteil ve Saint-Denis çoğunlukla göçmen nüfusun yaşadığı, Fransa geneline göre işsizlik oranının daha yüksek, ortalama gelirin ise düşük olduğu banliyöler. Olaylar boyunca adı sık anılan 2 bin öğrencili Paul-Éluard Lisesi de Saint-Denis’de bulunuyor. 2019’dan bu yana lisede çalışan Marianne Acqua adlı öğretmen liselilerin çok basit bir şey talep ettiklerini söylüyor:


“Onurlarına saygı gösterilmesi. Burada ders vermek, burada her gün eğitim görmek insanın onuruna yönelik bir meydan okuma. Okul binası tehlikeli derecede sağlıksız. Liselilerin burada gerçek anlamda bir kamu eğitim hizmetine erişebildiklerini iddia etmek, başlı başına bir hakaret.”


Lise bir süredir tadilatta olduğu için dersler prefabrik yapılarda sürdürülüyor. Öğrenciler yapıların yazın çok sıcak, kışın soğuk olduğundan yakınıyorlar.

“Okumak bir ayrıcalık değil, bir hak”

diyen 15 yaşındaki bir liseli

“Bu koşullarda nasıl konsantre olabilirsiniz?”

diye soruyor:

“İşçi sınıfı mahallelerinden geliyor olabiliriz, ancak diğerleri gibi bizim de haklarımız var. Medya bizi dersleri asmak, okulu yakmak isteyen vahşilermiş gibi gösteriyor. Yanlış! Biz sadece iyi koşullarda okumak istiyoruz.”


10 acil önlem


Öğretmen eksikliği nedeniyle boş geçen dersler, bakımsız okul binaları, yoğun çalışma programı, üniversite başvuru platformu Parcoursup’ün karışık yapısı özellikle banliyölerde yaşayan öğrencilerin dile getirdiği sıkıntılar arasında başı çekiyor. Eylemlerin yayıldığı günlerde öğrenci birlikleri change.org’da “Gençlik için 10 acil önlem” çağrısıyla imza kampanyası başlattı. Metindeki talepler şöyle:


Sağlıksız, harap durumdaki okulların yenilenmesi ve aşırı sıcak ve soğuk dalgaları gibi iklim değişikliğinin sonuçlarına uyumlu hale getirilmesi. Binaların bakımı ve sıhhi bölümlerin temizliği için gerekli insan kaynağı ve maddi koşulların sağlanması.


Eğitim, sağlık, destek ve rehberlik uzmanlarında kitlesel personel alımı. Her 500 öğrenciye bir hemşire, bir psikolog, bir rehberlik danışmanı. Eğitim kurumları arasındaki eşitsizliği sonlandırmak için kadrolu öğretmenlerin artırılması. Özel gereksinimli öğrencilere destek sağlayan eğitim asistanlarına resmi statü verilmesi ve 800 yeni kadro açılması.


Milli Eğitim Bakanlığı’nın Çocuğun Zamanına İlişkin Vatandaş Sözleşmesi’nden yola çıkarak okul programlarında köklü bir düzenleme yapılması, öğrencilerin ihtiyaçları ve esenliğine daha fazla özen gösterilmesi. En az bir saat 30 dakika öğle molası, lise ve lise bitirme sınavı (bac) reformunun yeniden gözden geçirilmesi.


Parcoursup ve Mon Master üzerinden seçimlerin sonlandırılması. Öğrencilerin algoritmik seçime maruz kalmadan üniversite ve yüksek lisansa devam edebilmeleri için 250 bin yeni öğrenci kontenjanı.


Lise öğrencilerinin karar alma süreçlerine katılabilmesi için öğrenci demokrasisinin elden geçirilmesi. Yüksek Eğitim Konseyi seçimlerinde her öğrencinin oy kullanabilmesi.
