author: groundxero
title: Where Women Make History: Reclaiming Agency in History and in Movements
content:
Gargi’s book is a historiographical recovery of the junctures when women fought and moved another inch towards occupying half the sky. 


 


By

 Vertika Mani 


 


The first intriguing thing to notice about V. Gargi’s

No Women, No History

 is the cover page of the book itself. Published by Virasam Books, the cover depicts women holding guns, marching with axes and also hugging trees. The image with its wide range of contrast yet a commonality of women as marchers and fighters interacts with its readers to convey the larger argument that this book seeks to make. The book was initially written as a collection of notes by V. Gargi, a revolutionary activist who dedicated this book

“To all the women who fought against overwhelming odds, made great sacrifices to the extent of even laying down their lives to make this place better for all of us…”


 


The first edition of

No Women No History: Women in Indian Movements (19th century – 2004)

 was published last year in August, at a pit stop, when the mainstream feminist discourse in India and abroad mostly associate women with power of intellect and pen, which are all quite a matter of privilege and can therefore be politically disabling at times. In that context, reading

No women No History

 is refreshing as it takes us down the road of history of women’s struggle, almost on a rampage to discover the truth of the fighting spirit that Indian women have always stood for.


 


An extraordinary range of political histories 


 


The book covers an extraordinary range of political histories and geographical contexts from 19th Century to the year 2004 covering histories of peasant and Adivasi uprisings, anti-caste struggles, labour movements, revolutionary politics, autonomous women’s organisations, ecological movements, struggles in the North-East, cultural organisations and contemporary campaigns. Its approach is broad and, for the most part, non-sectarian. Rather than treating “women’s issues” as a separate political category, Gargi locates women within the wider structures of social and political struggle, as peasants, workers, artisans, Dalits, Adivasis and members of minority communities.


 


This method of writing makes gendered oppression therefore appear not as an isolated structure but is seen in relationship with caste, class, feudal relations, economic exploitation and political power. This is among this book’s most important methodological contributions which allow the history of women’s liberation to be read as history of movements rather than that of organisations. A history of movements in which women fought over land, wages, labour, caste hierarchy, food, displacement, forests, political representation and state power. The breadth of the historical canvas is therefore significant to explore beyond conventional boundaries of women’s history.


 


Beginning with women’s participation in tribal and peasant rebellions, Gargi moves between the histories of Ranis and Begums and those of ordinary women who participated in the political ferment of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The juxtaposition prevents women’s history from becoming a gallery of exceptional female figures. It takes a dive into the political labour of ordinary women, particularly peasant, working-class, Dalit, Adivasi and other marginalised women, who have so frequently remained outside the central narrative of political history.


 


One of the salient feature of discussions around movements is the notable references made to the women pioneers, for instance, of Self-Respect Movement which is mostly associated with Periyar but more often than not misses to speak of Maniyammai, the woman who went on to lead the Kazhagam after Periyar’s death. Similarly, Gargi talks about Ambedkarite and Dalit movements including women’s role at length. Other such references include the distinctive forms of women’s participation in movements like Jail Bharo Satyagraha of 1960–65. The histories of women in the freedom struggle, women revolutionaries and communists are similarly placed alongside organisational histories that are less familiar in mainstream accounts.


 


Similarly, the book discusses collectives which are again, less talked about. For instance, The Mahila Atmaraksha Samitis (MARS), which emerged as an important form of women’s mobilisation before Partition. The further chapters trace the experiences of women during and after Partition, discovering a phase in history where …

author: CMI Argentina
title: El martirio de Nancy
content:
A Nancy Godoy el estado la dejó sola. Horas a caballo para llegar a su escuela, en medio de la nada, en el territorio de una estancia, que tenía dentro una escuela para sus peones. Llegó por primera vez y era una ruina. Lo denunció con detalles. La ignoraron. No llegó a cobrar un sueldo desde agosto. Apareció asesinada. Toda su lucha debió conocerse antes.


Por Silvana Melo


Nancy Godoy tenía ocho alumnos en una escuela pública dentro de una estancia. Es decir, en un territorio privado. Para llegar tenía que recorrer decenas de kilómetros de caminos rurales correntinos hasta ese punto de poder donde la alcanzaban hasta el paraje en el que un caballo la trasladaría durante tres horas para llegar a la escuela. Cruzando bañados, riachos y soledades escampadas que se volvían de una hostilidad imprevisible en caso de lluvias.


Tenía 52 años cuando ese 15 de agosto llegó a la escuela N° 626 del paraje El Malezal, en Esquina, Corrientes, para hacerse cargo de una suplencia. Era una casita desgastada, destruida, como si por ella hubiera pasado no sólo el tiempo, sino la desidia estatal y el desprecio privado.


Después de hacerse un panorama general de aquello a lo que se enfrentaba –suciedad extrema, ausencia de años de cualquier autoridad, falta de registros de todo tipo, situación sanitaria peligrosa, imposibilidad de habitar para ella, que debía quedarse la semana entera- el 15 de agosto escribió una carta manuscrita para enviar al ministerio de Educación de Corrientes. Y denunció cada detalle. Envió un expediente y sostuvo que la escuela estaba totalmente abandonada, sin agua, con inodoros llenos de tierra y ratas, que tuvo que acudir a una madre y a la baqueana que la acompañaba en el último tramo de su trayecto, María Rosa Leguizamón. En su casa tuvo que dormir las tres primeras noches porque la escuela era inhabitable. Esa misma mujer quedó involucrada después en la investigación por el crimen.


Decía que el techo se le caería encima, que las ventanas estaban rotas, que la humedad se comía el edificio, que las ratas y los murciélagos se habían apropiado de la casa, que el olor de sus heces era insoportable, que no había muebles suficientes, que los libros se habían mojado. Ella era docente, cocinera, portera y directora. Y era la responsable del edificio.


La carta que escribió Nancy a las autoridades educativas


Y la dejaron sola.


El estado la dejó sola. En medio de la nada, dentro de una estancia, en las manos de un propietario que hacía y deshacía, que tenía dentro de su propiedad una escuela para sus peones. Y ella debería comportarse como su maestra, directora, portera y cocinera. Con un sueldo pagado por el estado que la dejaba a la buena de dios. Sola de toda soledad.


Su denuncia fue ignorada por las autoridades educativas, sólo sostenida después de su desaparición por la comunidad de Esquina, sus docentes y su familia.


Pero esta lucha de ella debió conocerse antes de la tragedia.


No después. Cuando alguien la asesinó por el motivo que sea. Por ser mujer. Por ser maestra rural. Por tener coraje. Por denunciar.


Nancy se pasaba los días en esa escuela que tuvo que rehacer con sus manos y el fin de semana volvía con su familia. Sin señal de celular, sin comunicación de ningún tipo, su familia sabía que seguía viva cuando regresaba su sonrisa destruida por el cansancio. Pero aquel fin de semana no volvió. Y todo comenzó a volverse sombrío.


La dejaron sola. Tres horas a caballo y sin señal.


Apareció asesinada.


A metros del aula que había sabido reparar con sus manos, en la tapera del capataz, había ropa quemada.


Hay un estado que manda una trabajadora sola. A educar. Precarizada. A caballo. Sin señal de ningún tipo. Sin procurarle un transporte oficial. A que llegue como pueda. A una escuela en ruinas. Dentro de una propiedad de un estanciero. Ese estado cajonea su denuncia. Investiga su desaparición. Y la encuentra cuando fue asesinada.


En el territorio de la estancia El Curupí. En una escuela pública dentro de una zona privada.


El espacio Docentes Autoconvocados Corrientes – Sector 2019 aseguró que Nancy Godoy fue asesinada sin llegar a cobrar un solo sueldo a pesar de trabajar desde agosto.


A pesar del sacrificio para llegar. A pesar del desastre que encontró y del que nadie se hizo cargo. A pesar de que el docente que hacía años que no iba a la escuela seguía cobrando su salario.


Y ella fue asesinada por ser maestra en una escuela pública y tener que afrontar una realidad …

title: You can and should be able to construct your politics of trans liberation, including access to…
content:
tpwrtrmnky

:

You can and should be able to construct your politics of trans liberation, including access to transition care, gender marker change/abolition, all of it, independent of deference to any sort of “true gender” possessed by the individual. This is because the moment you say transness is contingent on having the right “true gender,” you open yourself to people trying to define the borders of who gets it and who doesn’t. A proper liberation framework says that everyone gets to transition as much or as little as they want to, no matter what.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: “My Body Is My Own”: Collective Memory, Remembrance, and Dignity in Taiwan Transgender and Intersex History
content:
This article submission was originally published by 跨服TransServer’s trans co-created column, Trans Day Reader and is syndicated here on New Bloom Magazine’s website with 跨服TransServer’s permission. In the original article, TransServer writes the following introduction:

November is Transgender Awareness Month and November 8th is Intersex Day of Remembrance. For the author, November 8th carries the weight of intertwined histories of medical violence within transgender and intersex communities, as well as the responsibility of building solidarity across these communities. Choosing this day to begin HRT, Yo-Ling offers this Trans Day Reader as an act of intervention, grounding its significance within the Taiwanese context.

The medical establishment profoundly impacts intersex well-being, as medical authority often overshadows bodily autonomy for intersex people. At the same time, scholars shape collective memory by ghostwriting for historical subjects. Positioned with critique and reflexivity, this article revisits archives of Mr. Xie Jianshun’s gender transition under duress, but more importantly, his acts of resistance, which advance a politics of self-respect for Sinophone trans and intersex communities. In reaching a wider public, readers must recognize academic critique as an autonomous domain and respect the author’s embodied self-disclosure.

NOVEMBER 8TH is both my gender affirming hormone therapy anniversary day, as well as Intersex Day of Remembrance. There is a story and a set of political reasons for choosing this particular date to start hormones. I am a Taiwanese transgender activist, as well as an independent scholar of transgender studies and Taiwanese postwar trans history. The first recorded use of hormones for gender transition in Taiwan is from the 1950s and was far from “gender affirming.” May this Trans Day Reader entry be a reminder to us all that holding our own collective memory is a form of resistance, especially when our histories have been written by scholars profiting off of our suffering, distorting and reproducing the realities of medical and archival violence, and damaging the intertwined dignity of Sinophone trans and intersex peoples.

On August 14, 1953, doctors at No. 518 Hospital of the ROC Army (陸軍第518醫院) in Tainan discovered that a soldier named Xie Jianshun (謝尖順) had intersex characteristics. The doctors performed an exploratory laparotomy on August 20 to determine Xie’s “true biological sex” and decided that he was anatomically “female” due to his having a uterus, two ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Doctors subsequently decided for Xie that he should receive “sex change” procedures, which included further surgeries and feminizing hormone therapy, in order to become a woman. [1] Xie expressed a strong desire to continue living his life as a man, even going so far as to tell reporters on August 21, after undergoing exploratory laparotomy, that he would rather kill himself than become a woman (United Daily News, 1953/08/21). Indeed, throughout the course of medical treatment and afterwards, archival materials surrounding Xie’s gender transition consistently demonstrate Xie’s self-conceptualization as a man and deep discomfort being both misgendered as and medically transitioned into a woman.

When Xie was ordered to be moved from No. 518 Hospital in Tainan to No. 1 General Hospital in Taipei (陸海空軍第一總醫院) later in 1953 to receive further “sex change” procedures, he told reporters that “I have already decided not to go up to Taipei. Whoever wants me to go to Taipei is better off sending me two bullets. I would rather die than comply. Although I am a soldier for whom obedience is my duty, my body is my own. I have the freedom to decide what to do with my own body” (Min Sheng Daily, 1953/12/09). Despite his explicit refusal, he was relocated to Taipei in early 1954 to continue receiving “treatments.”

In the fall of 1955, doctors at No. 1 General Hospital in Taipei decided for Xie that in order for him to “be able to become a mother” and have “menstrual bleeding that is the same as regular women,” and also for the sake of “achieving an even more tremendous advancement in medical research,” they would specially purchase injectable estrogen for Xie (United Daily News, 1955/10/15). Regarding how Xie felt about being injected with estrogen, news reports record him sharing “the pain of having needles inserted into [his] body is only secondary; watching [his] body change day by day is what …

author: Mekong Review 2
title: The state and the sin Rafly Gilang Pratama
content:
Calling themselves “boti hunters”, young men on motorcycles ride through dark alleys in Bogor targeting people they perceive to be queer. Credit: Dominic Kurniawan Suryaputra / Unsplash


T

he young men in the videos sounded as though they were having fun.


It was well past midnight in Bogor, Indonesia’s “rain city”. The roads were mostly empty and the boys rode motorcycles, looking for people they perceived to be gay, effeminate, or transgender. They revved their engines as they rode through the streets, shouting: “Bersih-bersih boti!”


“Clean up the boti!”


They proudly called themselves “boti hunters”, turning

boti

, a slang term derived from ‘bottom’, into the name of their little vigilante enterprise. There’s something accidentally homoerotic about groups of young men spending their midnight hours patrolling pitch-black alleys thinking about nothing but bottoms—but then someone in the frame starts running for their life, and the joke dies.


Accounts carrying variations of the “boti hunter” name soon appeared online. In the videos, the boys laugh and shout while they chase people through the streets, filming everything for a little bit of social media clout.


I’ve heard those laughs before.


I

 attended an elite, all-boys

pesantren

, an Islamic boarding school, in West Java. I entered primary school through a scholarship programme for

yatim

—children who had lost their fathers—and students from low-income families. By junior high, paying students from much wealthier families had joined us, many able to afford fees my family would have considered astronomical.


We joked that the pesantren was a “holy jail”: we were cut off from almost everything beyond the compound, our school surrounded by high walls with barbed wire. Our contact with the outside world was limited to about thirty minutes of restricted internet use at the end of computer class, Sunday family visits, and newspaper clippings pinned to noticeboards around the campus.


I remember how my friends and I were then. My roommates and I would steal (sorry!) the newspapers from the noticeboards and hoard the sports pages inside plastic binders. Our most prized trophy was a grainy image of Cristiano Ronaldo in his gloriously red Manchester United home kit. We loved the swagger, but mostly we loved that he belonged somewhere outside our cloistered world. One of my friends was from England—I called him “Brit Boy”—and some of the other kids would make fun of him for playing with us scholarship kids.


Twelve-year-old boys can be cruel. Hundreds of us living together, without girls or much privacy, meant that we turned our attention towards one another. As a scholarship kid whose father died when I was two, I learnt to harden myself. I had little in the way of a monthly allowance, and I didn’t receive the care packages that arrived for some of the other boys. I couldn’t compare with the rich kids who went on holiday and came back to school wearing the same bright Nike or Adidas shoes that professional footballers wore. I had no interest in becoming easy prey, so I tried my best to keep my head down.


One of the words we threw around was

banci

, a slur for boys thought to be too ‘feminine’. I had a friend who cared about his skin. We usually went straight to the mosque after our afternoon classes, carrying our bags with us at the end of the school day. One afternoon, he sat among us, putting something on his face. I don’t even remember what it was anymore, but that was enough. Suddenly, he was “banci” and the other boys were making fun of him. I laughed, too. I was scared of becoming the next boy people laughed at. At that age, drawing attention to myself felt like flying too close to the sun. Laughing along felt safer.


D

uring those years in school, we learnt the story of Prophet Lut and the destruction of Sodom. We heard frightening descriptions of stones, each engraved with a sinner’s name, falling from the sky, and the earth being overturned. We were taught that it was an azab, a divine punishment. By the age of nine, I had internalised the message that it was a sin for men to develop romantic relationships with other men, and that tolerating this sin would bring punishment upon everyone. It was only years later that I would encounter other interpretations of the story, including from progressive Muslim scholars, that centred coercion, sexual violence, and abuse of power.

title: Elaine Leeder - Anarcha-Feminismus
content:
Katalog Liste aller Texte AutorInnen Themen Letzte Einträge Zur Bibliothek hinzufügen

Mehr Kontakt Material Sticker, Plakate, etc.

Man sagt, daß Frauen oft Anarchismus praktizieren, ohne es zu wissen, während manche Männer sich selbst Anarchisten nennen, ohne das zu praktizieren. (…)

Es gibt eine Anzahl Feministinnen, die den unserer Entwicklung inhärenten Anarchismus erkannt und in Gruppenarbeit begonnen haben, zu lernen und zusammenzuwachsen als Anarcha-Feministinnen. Dieser „Zwitter“ entwickelte sich aus den späten 60ern heraus, als viele von uns in von Männern dominierten, nach „Wettbewerb“ und Hierarchie aufgebauten Massenorganisationen tätig waren. Zu der Zeit (und bis heute auch in der anarchistischen Literatur) wurde den Frauen gesagt, im Interesse der und für die große Bewegung zu arbeiten. Stattdessen bildeten wir kleine Selbsterfahrungsgruppen, die die persönlichen Fragen und Probleme unseres Lebens behandelten. Es waren spontane, auf „direkte Aktion“ zielende Gruppen: und für uns selbst organisiert. Sie ähnelten stark bestimmten Gruppen des Spaniens von vor 1936 und ließen sich als „affinity-groups“ bezeichnen.

Diese „affinity-groups“ gründeten sich auf gemeinsame Interessen und waren gekennzeichnet durch ein demokratisches Verfahren, in dem und durch das die beteiligten Frauen Information und Wissen teilten. Diese Gruppen setzten sich im allgemeinen aus weißen Frauen der Mittelklasse zusammen, die sich oft zum ersten Mal in einer Situation befanden, in der sie nicht miteinander zu konkurrieren brauchten.

Dritte-Welt- und Arbeiterklasse-Frauen waren normalerweise an solchen Gruppen nicht beteiligt; was auch heute noch die anarcha-feministischen Gruppen kennzeichnet. Was sich durch die Tatsache erklären läßt, daß diese Frauen – ausgebeutet als Arbeitskräfte und Minderheiten – mehr von Fragen und Aufgaben des Überlebens beansprucht waren.

Aus diesen frühen Anfängen entwickelte sich langsam eine feministische Theorie. Einige von uns in diesen kleinen Gruppen begannen, politische Theorie zu studieren und entdeckten den unserem Feminismus innewohnenden Anarchismus. Wir fingen an mit dem Gebrauch einer anarchistischen Analyse, die uns bei der Entwicklung einer Theorie und Strategie der Gesellschaftsveränderung helfen sollte. Wir machten uns klar, daß das Patriarchat eine von Männern beherrschte Hierarchie ist und daß die Kleinfamilie diese Hierarchie am Leben hält. Die Familie, so entdeckten wir, lehrt uns, Gott, den Lehrern, dem Chef und jedem sonst noch „Übergeordneten“ zu gehorchen. Sie drillt uns auf Wettbewerb, Verbrauch um jeden Preis, Isolation und den Umgang miteinander in einem Subjekt-Objekt-Verhältnis. Kleinfamilien, so wissen wir nun, sind die Basis aller hierarchischen, autoritären Systeme; und als Konsequenz: der Kampf gegen das Patriarchat ist ein Kampf gegen alle Formen der Hierarchie. Wenn wir die Natur der Kleinfamilie verändern, können wir auch beginnen, alle Formen des Führertums, der Herrschaft und der Regierung zu ändern.

Als ein Ergebnis dieser Form des Denkens legen Feministinnen nun Wert auf andere Wege, sich den Dingen zu nähern. Wir dürfen die Welt nicht länger nach dem Schema linearen Denkens sehen: rational gegen gefühlsmäßig, Verstand gegen Körper, Logik gegen Intuition. Wir haben begonnen, die Dinge, die Welt in einem Kontinuum als etwas Zusammengehöriges zu betrachten, statt sie in dualistische, auf Wettbewerb orientierte Teile zu „ordnen“. Wenn mensch sich der Welt konsequent auf diese Art nähert, wird klar, daß und warum Anarcha-Feministinnen nicht einen gleichen Anteil an der Macht für die Frauen fordern; stattdessen, daß alle Machtbeziehungen abzuschaffen sind. Wir wollen keine Frau als Präsidenten, wir wollen überhaupt keinen Präsidenten. Für uns ist „gleicher Lohn für gleiche Arbeit“ keine Kernfrage: Hierarchien und Machtverteilung dagegen sind es.

Es ist schon viel geschrieben worden über die Gemeinsamkeiten von Anarchismus und Feminismus. Beide, Anarchismus und Feminismus, ermutigen spontanen Wandel und freie Vereinigung. Beide sehen die Notwendigkeit von Massenbewegungen, aber nicht von Avantgarden und Führern. Beide ermutigen Wandel: von unten, nicht von oben. Anarchismus sieht als Feind den Staat; Feminismus sieht den Feind im Patriarchat. Anarcha-Feministinnen sehen beides als das gleiche an: Patriarchat ist ein nicht wegzudenkender Bestandteil des Staates. Wir bekämpfen denselben Feind an verschiedenen Stellen des zusammengehörenden Ganzen.

author: Paige Collings
title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
content:
What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?


Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. 


That's why earlier this year with the

queer arts collective

, we put out a

call for submissions

 inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom.


And we’re excited to share that the project is now live!

Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution. 


These essays and stories remind us that digital rights aren't just about the existence of technology and its deployment as existing in a vacuum, but instead about how tech tools are a way for people to express themselves freely, find communities, explore identities, and build spaces to exist and seek joy without fear. Too often, conversations about technology focus on innovation, efficiency, and the next big thing while overlooking the people and communities most affected by the systems being built. This project was an effort to break containment and make space for something different: a chance to imagine digital futures rooted in queer creativity, resistance, and possibility.


Together with the queer arts collective, we were excited to launch the magazine and celebrate the artists and ideas that brought it to life through our session at Mozilla Festival last week, ‘

Privacy x Queer Desire

,’ where we started out by co-curating a community privacy plan grounded in digital fairness before launching the magazine. 


If the stories in

Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 teach us one thing, it’s that we don't have to accept the digital future handed to us by oppressive governments and tech companies. We already have pre-Big Tech internet experiences encoded in our fondest memories that can inform our dreams for something better, and together we can build a new reality.

author: Erin Reed
title: There Are Plans to Defang or Defeat Anti-Trans Ballot Measures in Blue States
content:
Anti-trans ballot measures are barely passing — and they may not survive coming challenges.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Tuesday night, as election results poured in, it became immediately clear: anti-transgender ads had failed to earn Republicans a victory in the year they relied on them the most. Despite $183 million spent on ads targeting transgender people and any Democratic politician who had ever expressed support for them, even Democrats who openly supported transgender people won in Republican strongholds. As a trans woman won her race in a conservative Alabama district and fierce defenders like Peggy Flanagan won Minnesota’s U.S. Senate race, there was a lot to be hopeful about. But it was not all good news for transgender people on Tuesday night: results began to trickle in showing that anti-trans ballot measures were likely to pass in a handful of states, including blue states like Colorado and Washington. Though some of those vote totals remain uncertain, there is a significant likelihood that we will have our first anti-trans policies written into law in “safe states,” and there are already plans to ensure they never truly take hold.

In Colorado, a state many transgender people fled to because of its strong protective legislation, a sports ban and a surgery ban for transgender youth were ahead by razor-thin margins of 52-48. Neither has been called. Importantly, both measures are statutes, not constitutional amendments. That means the legislature can rewrite them, and it makes them ripe for challenge under the Colorado Constitution, in a state with strong legal protections for transgender people and a state Supreme Court that has enforced them, meaning the laws may never truly take hold. A state constitutional challenge would also be largely insulated from the U.S. Supreme Court: that case would run through the state court system, and the U.S. Supreme Court lets states interpret their own constitutions to protect more rights than the federal Constitution does.

In the meantime, transgender people can take heart that the measures, if they pass, will do so by very narrow margins. Transgender sports participation is not the “80-20 issue” some have claimed; this looks closer to a 50-50 issue. Voters also had relatively little time to learn what the laws would actually do. It remains to be seen what the impacts will be. Given how narrowly the measures appear to be passing, a strong campaign against them could conceivably defeat similar measures in the future, making state ballot measures far from the slam dunk anti-trans activists had envisioned.

Advocates and state leaders are not waiting for a court challenge, though. There is already talk of other ways to defang the measures. Colorado Governor-elect Phil Weiser said, “We’re going to have to take a look at these anti-trans measures and what adjustments are necessary and appropriate … It’s important that we recognize that sometimes, something is passed and it is incomplete. It is not administrable … it is a natural and, I believe, appropriate role for the legislature to say, ‘What are the adjustments that need to be added?’” And on the sports ban specifically, he said, “I don’t believe it would be acceptable to Colorado to have every student athlete to have to go through full-body examinations or other invasions of privacy.” What might this mean in practice? The measure itself never says how sex is supposed to be verified, so it could be defanged by allowing a birth certificate to serve as proof of sex in sports, a document that many states, including Colorado, allow trans people to change, or by allowing self-attestation to serve. And the legislature can and likely will adjust the law, meanwhile Colorado officials could put forward a non-enforcement agreement.

In Washington, similar dynamics are in play, and in fact the news may be a little more hopeful there. Initiative 638, which requires girls who want to play girls’ sports to get a statement from a health care provider verifying their sex, a requirement critics have warned could mean genital inspections, is passing 57-43 with plenty of the vote still out. Meanwhile, Initiative 1, the “parents’ bill of rights” that could have resulted in the forced outing of transgender youth, is trailing and seems likely to fail. author: TGEU
title: TGEU publishes Legal developments on trans-specific healthcare: A review of national case law in the EU
content:
Court cases have been central to advancing the rights of trans people in Europe, but trans-specific healthcare remains largely untested in the courts.


Since the European Court of Human Rights’ earliest decisions on legal gender recognition, strategic litigation has driven many major advances. More recently, rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union on freedom of movement and non-discrimination have further strengthened these gains. TGEU’s

2026 Trans Rights Map

 also found that national court decisions are increasingly driving progress in trans rights, particularly where legislative and policy advances are stalled or reversed.


Trans-specific healthcare is an exception and is comparatively less litigated at the European level. Trans people across the EU face significant barriers in accessing trans-specific healthcare. Enforcing their rights to healthcare is further complicated by administrative refusals, unclear national regulations, and national court rulings that remain largely unknown. At the same time, interest is growing in using legal tools to advocate for improved access to trans-specific healthcare, and in how courts across the region handle such cases.


get the publication


Objective of the publication


This resource explains how litigation can help improve access to trans-specific healthcare by reviewing case law from national courts across EU Member States.  Beyond resolving individual cases, court rulings can expand the scope of rights claims accepted and promote respectful, non-discriminatory language, even in complex areas like healthcare and health insurance law. 


We hope this resource empowers activists and lawyers to explore legal tools to improve access to trans-specific healthcare, drawing on ideas and arguments from similar efforts across the region.


What the publication covers


The publication presents national court decisions from EU Member States and covers key topics such as cost coverage, travelling abroad for care, age limits, waiting times, and discrimination. It includes cases where trans applicants won and cases where they didn’t, so readers can see what aspects courts consider relevant to their decision. Although the publication reviews case law in nearly all Member States, relevant cases were found in only a handful of countries, including Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, France, Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands.


get the publication


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Lulén y Max, dos jóvenes trans llevan año y medio encarcelados por defenderse de su agresor
content:
Lulen y Max son una pareja de dos personas trans condenados por intento de homicidio agravado con tentativa hacia el padre adoptivo de uno de ellos.

Los hechos habrían ocurrido en febrero del 2025 cuando ambos jóvenes se reúnen en la casa del padre de Lulen “Willian Watts” en Córdoba, con el motivo de buscar algunas reliquias de su abuela quién había fallecido recientemente.

El contexto de la familia adoptiva de Lulen es clave para entender los hechos, ya que desde su adolescencia se vio enfrentado a la violencia psicológica y física que perpetuaba el padre hacia la madre; a la homofobia del padre por su orientación sexual y posteriormente por su transición de género.

El día de los hechos como era recurrente hubo una discusión. Lulen y Max se defienden golpeando a Willian Watts hasta que un vecino escucha gritos, interrumpe la pelea y llama a la policía. Watts se encontraba inconsciente por una supuesta asfixia, pero queda vivo y sin lesiones. Desde ese día en febrero del 2025 Lulen y Max se encuentran secuestrados, presos en la cárcel de Córdoba.

La fiscalía les condenó a 12 años y seis meses de cárcel por intento de homicidio agravado con tentativa, primero por el vinculo familiar, segundo por alevosía y tercero por una supuesta teoría de premeditación (tentativa).

Sin duda ha habido diferentes vulneraciones desde el sistema judicial en su totalidad, ya que no dan ninguna relevancia a los hechos de violencia consecutiva y daños previos ejercidos por Willian Watts, tampoco otorgan valor al transodio y sostienen una hipótesis de película sin entender la legítima defensa y el malestar que puede llevar a una persona a defenderse.

En palabras de su red de apoyo:

“A pesar de que cayeron casi todos los agravantes que pidió el fiscal, la condena es insólita en su dureza y no se tuvieron en cuenta las circunstancias atenuantes que pidió la defensa; la de años de abuso y violencia psicológica hacia Lulén por parte de su padre.”

“Aún transitando el dolor y la bronca, estamos dispuestos a seguir a la próxima instancia judicial para lograr un mejor resultado. Seguiremos con actividades para terminar de juntar el dinero para terminar de pagar la defensa y vamos a sostener y abrir la campaña de libertad para Lulén y Max. Porque no aceptamos este fallo y no dejaremos que todo lo que se presenció quede impune.”

“Las vidas Trans importan, y ningún fiscal transodiante ni menos un tribunal discriminatorio nos van a parar o amedrentar.”

author: Clare Hymer
title: Could the Way the Greens Set Policy Be About to Change?
content:
Could the way the Green party of England and Wales makes policy – and who gets to call the shots – be about to change?


Ever since

the motion stating that Zionism is racism

 passed at Green conference in October, senior figures have taken to legacy media outlets to claim that the vote shows the party’s internal democracy isn’t working. 


In an act with more than a whiff of the Corbyn-era Labour right, former co-leader and MP for Waveney Valley Adrian Ramsay told Laura Kuenssberg at the weekend that the Greens are at risk of being overrun by the “hard left”. Ellie Chowns MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not

“vulnerable to capture by extremists”

, while Green trailblazer Caroline Lucas has raised

concerns about “entryism”

. 


But it’s not just the Greens’ old guard who think the party needs a shake-up. Leader Zack Polanski wrote in

a Guardian article

 after the conference that the party’s democracy must “evolve” to meet the Greens’ newly expanded membership, “creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set… strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible”. This was followed by

a “joint leadership statement”

 last week which said a working group had been set up, and the first proposals would likely be voted on at the party’s conference in spring 2027.


As it stands, the Greens have a one-member-one-vote system: any member, regardless of how long ago they joined the party, can vote on policy and changes to the party’s constitution. This direct democracy, which is distinct from the other mainstream parties in Britain, is cherished by the membership – and any group of members who organise well around conference can change party policy, be that to declare that Zionism is racism, or for the Greens

to ditch their longstanding opposition to nuclear power

. 


The recent murmurings around change have got some members worried. An

open letter

 to Polanski and co. circulating on social media this week insists that the party sticks with the one-member-one-vote model, and that “members will not accept any move away from this model”. Meanwhile, Greens for Palestine – the members behind the Zionism is racism motion – put out

a statement

 against those seeking to “subvert the Green party’s member-led democracy because they fear a loss of control”.


Russell Warfield, author of the new book

The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future

, told Novara Media he doesn’t think Polanski’s calls for improvements to the party’s democracy are, unlike for others, “a knee-jerk reaction to fix the ‘problem’ of the Zionism motion”. But for as long as the leadership’s proposals are unspecific, Polanski risks being seen to be in a coalition with those most vocally opposed to the motion. Members are likely wondering if their leader is –

like Ramsay

 – in favour of a delegate system more similar to Labour, whereby local parties select members to send to conferences.


On Wednesday, Greens Organise, a group of ecosocialist party members,

published a model motion

 aimed at improving how conferences run and better engaging members – one it hopes will be uncontroversial. It also

called for proposals

 for the more fundamental matter of how (and crucially if) the party’s democracy should be reformed. Co-deputy leader Rachel Millward told Novara Media the leadership welcomed this initiative, in addition to a forthcoming consultation of the wider membership.


Greens Organise said: “Any changes must serve the purpose of building a mass, ecosocialist party – not a reaction to any one policy… We should not leave it to [the leadership] to decide.”


The good news for those in the ‘change nothing’ camp is that anyone wanting to see a major reform through will have a tough time. First, they’d need a two-thirds majority. Second,

many have wrangled over the party’s internal workings before

 – and yet its core structure remains the same as 30 years ago. (Warfield noted that it’s an odd reversal that the veteran Greens “clamouring” for the current review “roughly correspond to the cohort who most resisted it last time”.)


“I think it’s unlikely this is going to be easily resolved,” Warfield said.

title: Alemania: la solidaridad con Palestina no es negociable
content:
Líder de Die Linke, Elif Eralp, y manifestantes pro Palestina en Alemania (Ibrahim Ibrahim entre ellos). Foto © Instagram / @eliferalp – Wikipedia


Die Linke fue la fuerza más votada en las últimas elecciones para la Cámara de Diputados de Berlín y de las asambleas de Consejales de Distrito el 20.09. Se desplegó una campaña de agresión, odio y mentiras, ya durante la campaña electoral, que se intensificó luego de la victoria. Obtuvo 25,7 % de los votos, seguido por CDU (derecha cristiana) con el 18,8 % y el partido Grün/Verde alcanzó el 14,3%. Pero como no se llegó a la mayoría, la izquierda podrá gobernar solo si se forma una coalición. CDU se negó rotundamnete a una coalción con la izquierda. Tras semanas de discuciones y peleas mediáticas, siguen sin ponerse de acuerdo sobre los puntos más candentes, que son los puntos claves, por los que muchas personas -sobre todo de origen migrante- habían depositado su voto a favor a Die Linke y son la no criminalización a la solidaridad con Palestina y la expropiación de los inmuebles.

Por Ana Muro, corresponsal de ANRed en Alemania.


El programa para las elecciones que presentó Die Linke decía entre otros puntos: “Deben fomentarse los proyectos contra el racismo antipalestino. Las restricciones a la libertad de expresión, de ciencia y de reunión, así como a otros derechos fundamentales, deben investigarse en profundidad en relación con esta forma específica de racismo y debe combatírselas.”


“La libertad de reunión debe protegerse con más fuerza frente a las restricciones estatales. (…) Condenamos la violencia policial y las restricciones desproporcionadas a la libertad de reunión y de expresión, como las que recientemente han afectado a manifestaciones solidarias con Palestina o aactivistas climáticos. (…) Queremos sacar a la autoridad de reuniones de la Policía de Berlín.”


El 8 de octubre se publicó el “acuerdo“ sobre el inicio de las conversaciones exploratorias entre Die Linke Berlín, Bündnis 90/Die Grünen y el SPD, entre los partidos que es posible una coalición. Ese acuerdo refuerza la represión, porque la definición de antisemitismo que utiliza es tan amplia que cualquier crítica a la política de ocupación, asentamientos, apartheid y genocidio del Estado de Israel queda incluida.


Ese acuerdo además fortalece a la policía y al Verfassungsschutz (Oficina para la Protección de la Constitución), amplía su presupuesto y sus competencias, y los refuerza como garantes de unapolítica de orden público que lleva tres años criminalizando y reprimiendo la solidaridad conPalestina.


Naturalmente los votantes se sienten traicionados


El acuerdo le da poder al SPD y a los Verdes, para decidir entre las voces aceptables y las que deben silenciarse, es decir, aquellas que no se ajustan a la Staatsräson, al apoyo incondicional de Alemania hacia Israel. Ambos partidos tienen una trayectoria bastante manchada en la historia. Los verdes en los 80′ empezaron militarizando la política exterior alemana y el SPD, a pesar de ser concebida con sociales, boicoteó la revolución en 1918 de la mano de Friedrich Ebert.


El arca política no quiere que gobierne un partido de izquierda, por ello a través de este acuerdo quieren un partido más débil, más dócil, divido, para poder frenar el tema que realmente le preocupa a la derechay al centro político: la expropiación de las viviendas. El monopolio inmobiliario tiene un poder inmenso y ejerce presión en los políticos.


La campaña de desprestigio a militantes concretos como Ferat Koçak y Vanessa Emde (ambos son los que más se solidarizan con Palestina) y a la izquierda en general, no apunta a combatir el antisemitismo real, sino a castigar cualquier voz que critique la política de ocupación, de asentamientos y de apartheid del Estado de Israel, o que cuestione la razón de Estado alemana. A su vez, se acusa a Die Linke por tener conecciones con Ibrahim Ibrahim e Issa Remo, ambos acusados de estar al frente de un clan criminal. Ibrahim Ibrahim es un activista de origen palestino y representante del Comité Nacional palestino unificado, se lo vincula con el Frente Popular para la Liberación de Palestina (considerada por EE.UU. y la UE como organización terrorista).


El tema Palestina, ya fue un punto de inflección en toda Alemania, pero también dentro de toda laIzquierda. Die Linke expulsó en 2025 a Ramsis Kilani, un activista de origen propalestino, su familia fueasesinada en un ataque aereo israelí en la franja de Gaza en 2014. Luego de más …

title: Özgür Sevgi Göral: France’s dilemmas also exist in Turkey - Part Two
content:
ANF spoke to academic Özgür Sevgi Göral, who is currently in Paris and has participated in the demonstrations, about the historical foundations of the protests and their potential.


Part one of this interview can be read

here

. 


When you compare these protests with the history of social movements and youth activism in Turkey, what similarities or significant differences do you see? Is the possibility of their influence spreading to Turkey limited, or what factors might increase that possibility?


This is a very difficult question. Youth movements in Turkey constitute a very broad field, and although I try to follow them, they are not my primary area of research. Therefore, I do not think I am in a position to compare the two countries in this respect. Perhaps I can offer just a few observations. Turkey has witnessed powerful youth movements, although they have been heavily suppressed, particularly over the past decade. We can assume that the racialised capitalist regime in which we live, and its various manifestations, have also generated considerable dissatisfaction among young people in Turkey. Moreover, even under Turkey's extremely harsh political conditions, youth movements have repeatedly emerged and made themselves visible over the past ten years. However, we know that for particular grievances or isolated political revolts to develop into powerful political mobilisation, there must be an accumulated history and tradition of struggle capable of protecting and developing itself. There must also be different political organisations operating at various levels, sometimes reaching agreements with one another and sometimes coming into conflict. I do not know to what extent such conditions exist or are possible in Turkey today, although there are certain emerging centres of struggle.


On the other hand, I think that rather than speaking of the protests spreading from one country to another, we can speak of a certain "simultaneity". Simultaneity, a concept frequently used in the literature on political and social movements, suggests that movements in different parts of the world during the same historical period can inspire one another in terms of political programmes, repertoires of mobilisation and demands, and that revolutionary ideas can travel across geographical boundaries. This could also apply to Turkey at a moment when the repertoire of street protests has some room to expand. However, the state's security strategy and policies against the accumulated experience of the Kurdish struggle, particularly the rapid criminalisation of forms of political violence and their framing through the concept of "terrorism", have unfortunately also proved effective among different political and social movements. Therefore, I cannot determine whether this wave of protests might produce rapid consequences for youth movements in Turkey through an effect of simultaneity, or what possibilities might exist for such a development. I am sure that my colleagues who are active in this field and study these movements have much more to say on the subject than I do.


Do these protests offer the prospect of lasting social and political transformation?


I think this question is extremely important, not only in relation to these protests but also in terms of the situation that widespread mass protests and uprisings have faced for some time. The latest youth uprising began on a broader scale than previous ones. However, in France and many other countries, it is debatable how successful such uprisings have been in producing concrete political and social transformation, despite all their potential. This movement also faces the dilemma your question points to. The central issue here is the dual nature of the demands of the groups driving the movement. There is a tension between those who prioritise short-term problems concerning the existing education system and those who focus on how wealth and resources should be distributed and on the broader prospect of anti-capitalist transformation. For now, it is difficult to say that this uprising has a programme and organisational structure based on a broader emancipatory perspective extending beyond its concrete demands. The government currently appears to have taken a step back by announcing that it will abolish Parcoursup, the university admissions system, in 2028. However, unless a strong and sustained bloc of political struggle can be established, it could introduce essentially the same …

author: Nick Everett
title: Will Israel’s election outcome make life better for Palestinians? Not likely.
content:
In the lead-up to Israel’s 27 October election, media headlines declared this would be the most “consequential” in Israel’s history. At stake is the fate of Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, who faces corruption charges at home and an international arrest warrant for war crimes in Gaza.

Israeli politicians debated the cost of living, the independence of the judiciary, conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the military, a state inquiry into security failings on 7 October and Israel’s growing isolation abroad. Not up for debate was Israel’s Gaza genocide, nor the massive expansion of Israeli settlements, settler violence and military invasions in the West Bank, nor Israel’s seizure of territory in southern Lebanon and Syria. 

This was a contest between two blocs, a pro-Netanyahu coalition of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties against an alliance of centrist and right-wing Zionist parties seeking to depose him, led by retired General Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff. A third bloc, made up of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, was initially barred from participation by Israel’s Central Elections Committee before the supreme court overturned the ban.

Right-wing parties Likud and Otzma Yehudit petitioned for their exclusion, accusing the Arab-majority parties and candidates of denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, supporting armed struggle against Israel or inciting racism. A ban was, however, upheld against Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party and one of the Joint List candidates, on the grounds that he had supported armed struggle against Israel. 

The evidence? An opinion piece published in 

Alaraby

 on 8 October 2023, in which Abu Shehadeh described the previous day’s Hamas-led attack on Israel as a “significant historical event”. 

Accusations of “inciting racism” against Ra’am and the Arab List are of course rank hypocrisy coming from Netanyahu and his coalition partners who have 

called for

 the “total annihilation” of Gaza’s cities and the burning of Lebanon, as well as the death penalty for Palestinians accused of “terrorism” offences.

On the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s social media posts drew attention to long queues of Palestinian voters at polling stations and urged Likud supporters to come out and vote.

“If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi”, he said, referring to the leaders of the two Arab-majority parties.

Netanyahu’s coalition ally and Jewish supremacist Itamar Ben-Gvir described the level of Arab voter turnout—people exercising their democratic right to vote—as “crazy”. As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has armed Israeli settlers and established a paramilitary police force in the West Bank.

Basel Smotrich, another Jewish supremacist Netanyahu ally, and leader of the Religious Zionism party, announced he had suspended his election day campaigning to convene an emergency meeting to discuss what he described as unusually high turnout among Arab voters, alleging voter fraud. 

While Netanyahu failed to win this election, he remains far from defeated. His ruling coalition, dominated by Likud, will likely secure 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, a major drop from the 64 seats he won in 2022, and significantly short of a majority. However, the opposition bloc is trailing with 48 seats. The opposition’s only pathway to power is to govern with the support of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, which together secured an additional 19 seats (nearly double the ten they secured in 2022).

This would not be unprecedented. In 1993, the Oslo Accords were signed by a minority Israeli government with the support of the Arab List parties.

In 2021, Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas broke with the Arab List to join an eight-party coalition, the first time an Arab-majority party had joined an Israeli government. For Abbas, this was an opportunity to secure some short-lived investment in Palestinian communities inside Israel, while turning his back on the elephant in the room: the Israeli occupation. The coalition collapsed within a year following defections from its right flank.

Abbas has declared his intention again to seek a coalition that can unseat Netanyahu. His Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on its slate. However, such overtures have so far been rebuffed.  …

title: Fransa'da ırkçılık ve İslamofobi karşıtı gösteriler düzenlendi
content:
Fransa'da farklı sendika, dernek ve kitle örgütü kuruluşlarının çağrısıyla Paris, Strazburg, Roubaix, Stains, Nanterre, La Courneuve dahil farklı kentlerde ırkçılık karşıtları bir araya geldi.

Ülkede artan ırkçılığa ve İslamofobiye tepki verilen gösterilerde, 23 Ekim'de Yvelines ilinde düzenlenen terör saldırısında hayatını kaybeden Kongo asıllı Fransız Pengo Bossio Wangi anıldı.

Gösterilerde, söz konusu ırkçı saldırıda yaralanan 1'i çocuk olmak üzere 5 kişiye yönelik destek mesajları da dile getirildi.

Başkent Paris'te Stalingrad Muharebesi Meydanı'nda yerel saatle 19.00'da başlayan gösteriye yüzlerce kişi katıldı.

Göstericiler, "Irkçılık bir görüş değil, hayatları paramparça eden bir suçtur", "Paramparça olan hayatlardan ziyade kırılan vitrinlere şefkat gösteriyorlar" ve "Irkçılık öldürür" yazılı pankartlar taşıdı.

Göstericiler, ırkçı söylemleri yaymakla suçlanan CNews kanalında çalışan bir gazetecinin gösteriye katılmasına "CNews dışarı" ve "CNews katil, (Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel) Macron suç ortağı" sloganları atarak tepki gösterdi.

Irkçılıkla mücadele derneği SOS Racisme'in Başkanı Dominique Sopo, burada yaptığı konuşmada, birkaç yıldır ülkede ırkçı saikli suçların yeniden işlenmeye başlandığını söyledi.

Sopo, bazı medya organlarının bünyelerinde ırkçı söylemlerin sarf edilmesine izin verdiğini belirterek, bu söylemin son derece "ciddi" olduğuna dikkati çekti.

Yvelines'e bağlı Trappes kentindeki saldırıyı yapan teröristin "siyahilere ve Araplara saldırarak 17 Ekim'deki gösterilerinde, dükkanı yağmalanan esnafın öcünü almak istediğini" dile getirdiğini aktaran Sopo, terör saldırısından birkaç gün önce Fransız televizyon kanallarında eylemlerdeki yağma olaylarıyla ilgili ırkçı bir çerçeve kullanıldığını belirtti.

Trappes Belediye Başkanı Ali Rabeh ise Ulusal Birlik (RN) Partisi Başkanı Jordan Bardella'nın daha önce Trappes kentini "Paris'e 30 dakika mesafedeki Kabil'e" benzettiğini hatırlattı.

Rabeh, Trappes'a yönelik damgalayıcı sözler kullananları terör saldırısının failine silah vermekle suçlayarak, "Kanallarda durmaksızın aktarılan yabancılara, göçmenlere, Müslümanlara karşı sarf edilen nefret söylemleri, Fransızların bir kısmının insanlıktan çıkarılmasına neden oldu." dedi.

Bu durumun, bu kişilerin "iç düşmanlar" gibi gösterilmesine sebebiyet verdiğini kaydeden Rabeh, ırkçılık zehrinin tüm ülkeye bulaştığını dile getirdi.

Irkçılık Karşıtı Koalisyon'dan yapılan açıklamaya göre, Paris'te Cumhuriyet Meydanı'nda düzenlenmesi planlanan bir diğer gösteri, Paris Emniyet Müdürlüğünce yasaklandı.

Sosyal medyaya yansıyan görüntülere göre, bazı göstericiler, yasağa rağmen Cumhuriyet Meydanı yakınlarında toplandı.

Sokakta yere oturan göstericiler, Fransa'nın ulusal marşı La Marseillaise'i okudu.

Polis, eylemi dağıtmak için kalkanlarıyla göstericileri iterek bölgeden uzaklaştırmaya çalıştı.

Yvelines ilinde 23 Ekim'de bir kişi, bulunduğu araçtan etraftakilere ateş açmıştı. Saldırıda 1 kişi hayatını kaybetmiş, 5 kişi ağır yaralanmıştı.

39 yaşındaki saldırgan Kevin T, olay yerinde gözaltına alınmıştı.

Fransa Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel Macron, saldırının ırkçı nitelikte bir terör saldırısı olduğunu duyurmuştu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: [Valladolid] Apertura de nuevo local de CNT
content:
Antifascistas, antirracistas, anticapitalistas, transfeministas e internacionalistas. En medio de una convocatoria de huelga general por la vivienda y contra todos los poderes que viven de desangrar a la clase trabajadora, CNT Valladolid inaugura un nuevo local en calle Merced, 6, de Valladolid, entre las plazas de Santa Cruz y Circular.


Hace más de dos años empezamos un proyecto muy ilusionante. Nuestro local se quedaba pequeño y teníamos que buscar otro. Hicimos un proceso de reflexión colectiva, para tener claras nuestras necesidades presentes y futuras. Una tienda de fontanería se ha convertido en un sindicato como el nuestro, con más salas donde reunirse, un salón amplio en el que convocar actos… Un nuevo espacio en Valladolid a disposición de todas las personas trabajadoras.


A pesar de que quedan retoques, el pasado 17 de octubre nos decidimos a abrir puertas en un acto en el que nos reunimos la afiliacIón con personas afines del presente y del futuro. Contamos con las actuaciones de Jesús Puebla Mimo, de Rubén Ruiz, Rosa Vicente y José Luis Alonso, de Chusma y de Juguillos, de Astrolabio, y tuvimos ocasión de mover el esqueleto con las aportaciones de Eva DJ. No faltaron el recorrido por el nuevo local, el picoteo hecho a mano en comida y bebida, y sobre todo las ganas de llenar de vida esta nueva casa para la rebeldía y la defensa frente a empresaurios y politicastros de todos nuestros derechos actuales y los que nos inventemos en el futuro. Para todo ello y más, contad con CNT, vuestra herramienta de lucha, vuestro sindicato de clase, vuestra alternativa sindical.


A continuación hemos puesto en marcha unas jornadas de inauguración de las que tenéis información en las redes y web de CNT.


Reproducimos a continuación el manifiesto que refleja esta nueva etapa:


Hoy, sábado, 17 de octubre, inauguramos una nueva etapa en CNT Valladolid.


Estrenamos un espacio más amplio. Un espacio donde pueda entrar más gente, donde podamos encontrarnos, organizarnos y construir juntas una respuesta colectiva a la realidad que vivimos.


Porque este local no es solamente un lugar nuevo. Es un espacio de encuentro para quienes entendemos que nuestros derechos no son concesiones, que la dignidad no se negocia y que nuestra fuerza está en la lucha obrera.


Y cuando decimos clase trabajadora, no hablamos solo de quienes tienen un contrato o un empleo. También hablamos de quienes trabajan sin derechos, de quienes sostienen los cuidados y de quienes encuentran las puertas cerradas al empleo por su identidad o su condición.


Porque si el sistema utiliza esas diferencias para dividirnos y para colocar a unas personas en posiciones de mayor vulnerabilidad, el sindicalismo tiene que hacer justamente lo contrario:

reconocernos como parte de una misma clase y organizarnos juntas.


Por eso abrimos este espacio.


Para que haya más gente, más organización y más lucha.


Porque somos CNT.


CNT tiene una historia profundamente ligada a la organización de la clase trabajadora y a la lucha por los derechos laborales y sociales.


Antes que este local, CNT tuvo varios, cada uno con su historia: desahucios, asaltos policiales, atentados… Desde la calle Francisco Zarandona multiplicó por diez su afiliación en tiempos de la segunda republica; desde los pactos de la moncloa, superando multiples dificultades, hemos crecido en varios locales en Valladolid que han ido abriendo cada vez más brecha en la provincia y en la ciudad. Hasta llegar a este en el que nos encontramos


Somos anarcosindicalistas. Entendemos que quienes vivimos de nuestro trabajo tenemos capacidad para defender nuestros derechos colectivamente y para construir otras formas de relacionarnos y organizarnos frente a la explotación.


Tenemos una memoria sindical fuerte y combativa. Pero no queremos convertir esa memoria en una fotografía, ni mirar hacia atrás únicamente para recordar lo que fuimos.

Nuestra memoria nos obliga a mirar hacia delante.


Porque el sistema contra el que se organizaron quienes nos precedieron no ha desaparecido. La explotación adopta nuevas formas. La precariedad se normaliza. Trabajar ya no garantiza unas condiciones de vida dignas. Y quienes acumulan riqueza siguen teniendo capacidad para decidir sobre nuestras vidas.


Por eso estamos aquí.


Porque la lucha sigue.


Y esa lucha sigue hoy en múltiples frentes que se complementan.


Una de ellas es la

lucha antifascista

.


Estamos viendo crecer discursos que alimentan el odio y el miedo …

author: Unknown
title: Saki: Turkish citizens top the list of deportations from Europe
content:
Deportations across Europe have accelerated following the implementation of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum. These measures have begun to affect not only undocumented migrants but also asylum seekers and political refugees who have been granted asylum.


The adoption of the pact has been followed by an increase in deportation orders targeting Kurdish refugees in particular. Numerous Kurdish political refugees have begun to be returned to Turkey from the European countries where they reside. Refugees, including politicians, poets and writers, face trials carrying potential prison sentences of several decades under cases brought against them after their return to Turkey.


Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP Özgül Saki spoke to ANF about recent developments affecting migrants in Europe and the growing number of deportation orders.


'The price of the crisis is poverty, massacres and displacement'


Özgül Saki said that pressure on refugees had intensified following the implementation of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum on 12 June 2026. She added said: "Following its entry into force on 12 June, the Council of the European Union (EU) formally adopted a new regulation known as the Return Regulation on 1 October 2026, aimed at accelerating the deportation and return of irregular migrants who have no legal right to remain.


We must first recognize that since 2013, we have been witnessing mass migration on a scale unprecedented in previous periods. The period of conflict that began with ISIS attacks in Syria and Iraq, Israel's genocidal policies against Palestine, the escalation of tensions between Ukraine and Russia into a prolonged war, the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan and US attacks on Iran have displaced millions of people. In my view, the underlying cause is the imperialist capitalist system's continued reliance on war as a regional strategy to resolve its own crises. The price of this crisis continues to be paid by the peoples of the region through poverty, massacres and displacement.


We are witnessing the re-emergence of colonial reflexes. Efforts to remain protected within Europe's own borders are proceeding alongside expansionist ambitions beyond them. Concepts described as 'European values,' such as human rights, democracy and equality, have lost their meaning. We are confronted with a Europe dominated by governments that regard everything as permissible in the name of 'security' and 'defense,' are turning toward fascism and envision a white Europe.


There is a widespread expectation that migration statistics will increasingly be used as a political tool, particularly amid the rise of the far right in Germany, the Netherlands and France. The prominence of 'returns,' 'border security' and 'irregular migration' in election campaigns indicates that this right-wing and fascistic trajectory will continue. As a result, a deliberate anti-migrant political agenda is being implemented through new, multilayered mechanisms of pressure on refugees."


'Restrictions begin at the border'


Özgül Saki said that, according to the Council of the European Union, the regulation adopted on 1 October expands member states' powers to carry out deportations.


Saki continued: "We have already begun to see the serious consequences of the new legislation in recent months. The coming period will bring highly unfavorable conditions both for migrants already living in European countries and for those seeking to apply for asylum.


The Council of the European Union stated that the new rules adopted on 1 October will complement the Pact on Migration and Asylum and contribute to its implementation. The regulation gives member states greater scope to carry out returns and allows for the establishment of 'return hubs' in countries outside the EU. author: Justin Garson
title: Seeing BPD in a Positive Light: An Interview with Dr. Shay Welch
content:
P

eople often take psychiatric drugs because there’s something about themselves they don’t like—extreme low mood, threatening voices, or panic attacks. But many who’ve been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD) take drugs for the sake of others. They’re repeatedly told that their very personalities are disordered, pathological or just intolerable. This message is profoundly stigmatizing. It can contribute to isolation, loneliness, and even suicidal thoughts.


In September 2024, I talked with

Dr. Shay Welch

, a philosophy professor at Spelman College. Welch, who’s been diagnosed with BPD, truly writes from an insider’s perspective—a perspective that’s nearly absent from the academic literature.


Shay Welch


Her recent paper, “

Am I Safe Enough for You Now? BPD and the Forced Erasure of Personal Identity

,” describes how people with BPD often feel forced to erase who they are to make others feel safe. We discuss ways of promoting more positive messaging around BPD, and creating a more tolerant and accepting society.


The title of her paper captures a theme that ran throughout our conversation: “treatment” for BPD is often less about alleviating the diagnosed person’s suffering than about making them more tolerable to other people. She describes medication levels that kept rising to make other people more comfortable, and a research literature built almost entirely around people in crisis. She also describes what would make life better: a cultural shift that would see, in BPD, not a defective kind of person, but just a different kind of person.


Justin Garson: There’s this idea that people take psychiatric drugs to manage parts of themselves that are inherently distressing, like being depressed or anxious. But as you point out in your paper, people with BPD often take medications for the sake of others. You describe how other people want to “erase—literally—who we are for their own comfort.” Can you say more about this idea of taking drugs to erase one’s personality?


Shay Welch:

 It’s true that you have these categories of social anxiety, panic attacks, and chronic deep depression, and those can interfere with somebody’s ability to thrive. But then you have these “identity” disorders, like BPD and bipolar and schizophrenia, which make other people very uncomfortable. When it comes to bipolar, or BPD, or schizophrenia, the institutions or the medical field itself will try to medicate it completely out of them. And then you just completely eliminate the person. These people are like, “I’m not a person. I am so medicated, I don’t exist as an individual.”


So, we are constantly trying to back off the medication to hit a point where we’re still satisfying other people, but reclaiming more of our actual identity. But that’s when people say, “you’ve come off your meds too much, and now you’re not functioning well in society and you need to go back on your meds.” And then people like us are like, what do I do? I’m terribly unhappy, but it’s me versus all of them. That causes many people to isolate themselves.


For example, a lot of bipolar people really love their mania. They accomplish so much, and their lives are so colorful, when they’re in the manic state. Then they have to go into the depression state. But sometimes they’ll tolerate the depression for the mania—especially if your manic state is longer than the depressive state. But other people don’t like that. For others, it’s too intense or erratic.


Garson: That makes sense. My dad was bipolar and he was on medication mainly because people didn’t like his manic episodes. In general, he didn’t like medication—he enjoyed having those emotional extremes.


But it seems to me—and this is something you get at in your paper—that for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, there’s a sense that “we’re treating your symptoms,” like hallucinations or manic episodes. Whereas for BPD, the “problem,” as it were, is you. The message is that your very personality is at fault.


Welch:

Right. What makes these “personality disorders” is that there’s a problem with your personality. I’ve often been told that I’m too boisterous for other people. Even when I medicate, I project my voice. I’m very straightforward and very blunt, but I’m always enthusiastic, like, let’s go. I’m driven. Before I was medicated, people didn’t like that.


And it’s true that when you’re not medicated for borderline, you do have these spillovers. I spent my whole life having random …

title: In Their Own Words: The Senior Reform and Tory Figures Who Have Lauded Trump
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump suffered a spectacular setback in the country’s midterm elections this week, with Democrats taking control of Congress and the Republicans losing races in their traditional heartlands.


The election was a rebuke to Trump’s increasingly

unpopular presidency

. Voters expressed frustration with the cost of living and the economy, while the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran – which has driven up fuel prices – has proven to be a major political liability.


Trump’s political fortunes have also been damaged by his administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency at the centre of his mass deportation drive, has become a flashpoint and an emblem of Trump’s autocratic rule.


Yet, across the Atlantic, some of the UK’s most senior right-wing politicians have spent recent years enthusiastically praising Trump, celebrating his political leadership, and seeking to emulate his policies.


Reform UK

Nigel Farage

With Reform
