author: Chris Walker
title: Muslim, Jewish Groups Warn “Right to Worship” Bill Could Undermine Free Speech
content:
“Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights,” the groups explained.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Two religious organizations — one Jewish and one Muslim — are urging lawmakers to reject a bill that ostensibly aims to protect houses of worship but that would actually quell free speech rights.

“The Right to Worship Act,” sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and cosponsored by Republicans and Democrats alike, seeks to “protect” religious buildings and people inside them by limiting the First Amendment right to protest in nearby areas.

The bill prohibits activities within 100 feet of a house of worship that include actions that are “knowingly disrupting the scheduled religious service” or “impeding people from participating at [a] scheduled religious service.”

While the legislation limits protections to the period of time “beginning 1 hour before the start of and ending 1 hour after the conclusion of a scheduled religious service,” the ambiguous language of the bill could feasibly allow houses of worship to define almost any event as being “protected” from demonstrations happening nearby — for example, a church bake sale could be considered a “scheduled religious service” by some, as could a political event featuring a controversial speaker discussing religious topics.

“Offenders” could be fined $2,500 by the federal government for their first instance of violating the rules laid out in the bill, and up to $10,000 for subsequent violations. The bill also grants private individuals who feel that their religious rights have been violated the ability to sue for “damages” of up to $5,000 per violation.

While most sponsors of the bill are Republican, it does have bipartisan support. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) has signed on as a cosponsor, and 13 Democrats are cosponsors of the House version of the bill.

The Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC) and Bend the Arc: Jewish Action issued a joint statement urging lawmakers to reject the legislation, arguing that it sacrifices protections for one fundamental liberty to provide unnecessary protections for another.

“As Muslim and Jewish organizations, we understand the urgent need to protect houses of worship from threats, violence, intimidation, and physical obstruction,” the statement from the two groups explained. “Every person deserves to practice their faith freely and safely. However, protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights.”

The organizations argued that the broad language of the bill risks “chilling lawful speech, peaceful assembly, and political protest, including on public sidewalks and streets.”

“The legislation fails to adequately distinguish between genuine threats to religious exercise and constitutionally protected expression,” they said, adding:

Our communities know firsthand the consequences of religious hatred and discrimination. We reject the notion that protecting Muslim and Jewish Americans requires weakening the constitutional freedoms that safeguard us all.

The groups are calling on other members of Congress to reject the bill, and in the future, for lawmakers to only “pursue narrowly tailored protections that safeguard religious communities without restricting lawful expression.”

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) has also condemned the bill, warning that it could limit speech protections for protests outside religious venues that are hosting Israeli settlement land sales, further promoting dispossession of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

In an explainer on the legislation published in September, CAIR labeled the bill as essentially an “Illegal Israeli Settlements Protection Act” that, if enacted into law, could be used to “discourage lawful demonstrations against events promoting Palestinian dispossession.”

“Existing federal law already prohibits force, threats of force, and physical obstruction directed at religious worship,” the organization said in a statement. “CAIR therefore questions the need for a new civil-liability regime that could be used to burden constitutionally protected advocacy and dissent.”

“Hosting a political or commercial event in a religious building should not shield that activity from public accountability,” CAIR added.

author: Rory Mir
title: Google Forcing AI on Students Is BS
content:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.


Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini

for 150 million K-12 students

 on Google Classroom, leaving educators

scrambling to respond

. A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators

would also be turning off Google search

.


Google

walked this back

 somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.


Tying AI to Search


It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI  are

operating at a huge loss

, in the hope they can follow


Uber’s enshittification playbook

. Offer a cheap convenience

at a major loss

 until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data. 


This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around

90% of search traffic

. It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in

clumsy self-preferencing

 that is

eating its own ad revenue

.


The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned 

about the accuracy of AI overviews

 or their

impact on click-through rates

 for

online communities

 and

small publishers

 can just

deal with it

. The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.


Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links. 


It’s not enough to point to

opaque workarounds

, either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to

settings for system administrators

. Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.


Pushing AI on Schools


De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem

despite data privacy concerns

. That’s because schools face major

switching costs

 when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work. 


The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to

AI-driven schools

, but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing

major school districts

 to implement temporary

AI moratoriums

 for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI 

fits the needs of students


and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared. 


But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their …

author: Mitch Perry
title: CAIR Ends Operations in Florida as “Domestic Terrorist” Designation Takes Effect
content:
Gov. Ron DeSantis has been attempting to put the Muslim civil rights organization out of business for nearly a year.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR) has suspended operations in Florida, the organization has announced.

It did so after a federal judge rejected an emergency request Wednesday by the Muslim civil rights organization to stop the state from designating the group and its state chapter as domestic terrorist organizations, allowing the designation to take effect while its legal challenge, litigated by the ACLU and the Southern Poverty Law Center, continues.

Federal Judge Allen C. Winsor of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida denied CAIR and CAIR Florida’s request to reverse the designation. In a ruling released Wednesday night, Windsor said the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed at this stage on their claims that the designations under a new law (HB 1471) violates their due process and First Amendment rights.

The judge did issue a narrow form of preliminary relief, stating that Florida prosecutors cannot enforce the law against CAIR and CAIR Florida, their employees, or third parties with respect to provision of legal services to the groups.

That designation took effect Thursday. As a result, both groups say they have been forced to shut down their advocacy and operations in Florida.

“Today’s ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project.

“Today’s decision upholds state officials’ sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorist,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. Florida officials have been relentless in seeking to silence our clients’ civil rights work and advocacy, damaging not only them but also their community. We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier hailed the ruling Thursday. “Great win by our Solicitor General’s office and for the people of Florida!” Uthmeier wrote on X.

DeSantis and other members of the Florida Cabinet voted to designate CAIR and CAIR Florida as domestic terrorist organizations on Sept. 29. They contend the group operates as a front for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood.

Attorneys for CAIR have vehemently denied the allegation, contending its mission, “rooted in faith, is to enhance the public’s understanding of Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice and empower American Muslims.”

The designation in late September came months after DeSantis signed legislation approved by the Legislature earlier this year that gave five Florida executive officials — the head of domestic security (the commissioner of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement), the governor, and the three members of the state Cabinet — power to designate and eliminate groups operating in the United States without filing any legal charges or submitting their case to a jury.

The legislation prohibits any state agency, political subdivision, or public school district from expending or accepting state funds to support groups thus designated. It bans public schools or school districts from spending state or federal funds or maintaining programs on campus that “promote” a designated group.

The law also says any college or university must report information relating to the status of a student attending that school on a student visa if the student “promotes” a terrorist-designated organization. Students found to have promoted the group can be expelled.

The ACLU, the ACLU of Florida, and two other legal groups representing CAIR and CAIR Florida filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the legislation in July in the Northern District.

“As Florida chief of domestic security, I know there are imminent dangers to public health, safety, and welfare due to increasing risks from foreign and domestic terrorist groups,” then-FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass said on Sept. 11. Glass has since been replaced by Larry Keefe.

DeSantis has been attempting to put CAIR out of business for nearly a year. He issued an executive order in December designating CAIR and CAIR-Florida as terrorist organizations, directing state and local agencies to block them and their supporters from public contracts, funding, and benefits. title: AIPAC Has Lost Over 30 of Its Midterm Races So Far, In Sign of Major Shift
content:
Roughly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable lobbying group this cycle went toward races they lost.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has lost dozens of races in which it backed a candidate in this year’s midterm elections, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable political lobbying group, in a sign of its waning influence.

Politico found in a report on Thursday that more than 30 of the group’s candidates lost their elections this week. This marks “defeat for AIPAC in over three-fourths of the competitive races that have been called so far where it backed an incumbent,” Politico reported.

This includes candidates like Republican Representatives Mike Lawler (New York), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), and Max Miller (Ohio), as well as Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who fell to progressive Israel critic Troy Jackson, and Mike Rogers in Michigan.

Collins has been a staunch defender of Israel in the Senate, and AIPAC was her biggest outside donor by a massive margin during the race. AIPAC gave $2.8 million supporting her race against Jackson, as data from OpenSecrets showed; the next-largest outside donor, investment firm KKR & Co., gave just a fraction of that, at $160,000.

AIPAC dumped even more money into the race against Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, whose opposition to the U.S.-Israel relationship has been a hallmark of his campaign. AIPAC and its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), reportedly dropped up to $9 million supporting Rogers in the last weeks of the election. This came after AIPAC spent a whopping $30 million opposing El-Sayed and backing Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan) in the primary.

The next largest target after El-Sayed was Daniel Biss, who won his election to the U.S. House in Illinois after UDP dumped $6.3 million against him. Biss explicitly ran on a platform opposing AIPAC and its influence.

These losses are staggering for a political group whose name was once synonymous with power in D.C. In fact, these results indicate that being affiliated with the group is becoming politically toxic, due in large part to the work of pro-Palestine advocates who spoke out against the group amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

AIPAC, perhaps concerned about losing donors, defended its record on X, arguing that it backed 245 candidates who won their races. But the contributions to these races represented only about a third of their spending in this cycle.

According to Responsible Statecraft, almost two-thirds of the money that AIPAC and UDP spent this cycle went toward losing candidates. Via UDP, AIPAC spent $84.1 million on elections — $55.3 million of which went toward races where their preferred candidate lost. This stands in sharp contrast to prior election cycles. In the 2022 midterm election, Responsible Statecraft found, 69 percent of UDP spending went toward races their candidate won. In 2024, their winning ratio was 87 percent.

AIPAC can still wield enormous power over Congress. In its first post-election post on social media on Wednesday, the lobbying group congratulated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) for the “resounding victories for their caucuses.” The lawmakers are currently poised to lead the House and Senate when the new Congress begins in January, and are two of Israel’s staunchest defenders in Congress and major allies of AIPAC.

But the sands are quickly shifting under their feet. Opposing Israel and AIPAC have become increasingly normalized positions for politicians as the public overwhelmingly rejects the U.S.-Israel relationship, with even candidates in deep red states running against the lobbying group.

In Mississippi, for instance, Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom pledged to never take AIPAC money. He is currently holding on to a narrow lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Mississippi) in their election, and, if he wins, will be the first Democratic senator elected from the state since 1989.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: It Wasn’t Just Gas Prices. Anti-ICE Sentiment Fueled Republican Midterm Losses.
content:
Polling finds that Americans across racial and ethnic groups view ICE more unfavorably today than they did a year ago.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

While President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance blame Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections on their war on Iran — with Trump flippantly saying that the war “drove the gasoline up a little bit short term” — Tuesday’s results also represent a rejection of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In Texas, where Trump won a Latino majority in the presidential election in 2024, the midterms saw a reversal, with Latino votes playing a role in the victories of Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa. Polls show 6 in 10 Latino voters supporting Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton — and in South Texas, Talarico performed better than Democrats have since the 1930s.

Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) said that “we haven’t seen this huge a Latino voter surge before,” and stated that “the difference is ICE and the mass deportation campaign.” Talarico had spoken against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, and against ICE’s tactics.

ACLU Texas polling prior to the midterm elections showed that 53 percent of residents in Texas border regions feel that immigration enforcement has made life harder, rather than making their communities safer. The polls also showed that 63 percent of those residents believe that ICE tactics “have gone too far.”

One resident surveyed in the poll — which spoke to 1,031 adults in El Paso and Rio Grande Valley counties — said that “ICE isn’t helping by deporting our hardworking immigrants regardless of their status. This whole region and country has been built on the backs of immigrants.” The resident had voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

In Maine, too, voters expressed that the ICE crackdown over the past year had pushed them to vote against Republican Sen. Susan Collins, with the ICE killing of Johan Sebastian Guerrero in July as a particular flashpoint. Residents asked why Collins had not done more to stop ICE’s violent raids — and why she instead voted for more funding for the agency.

Democrat Troy Jackson, on the other hand, has said that he will “fight to abolish ICE.” In his victory speech on Wednesday, he said: “Masked agents terrorizing our neighbors and ripping families apart should never be accepted in the United States of America.”

And in Minnesota, the site of ICE’s “Operation Metro Surge” at the beginning of the year, which saw federal agents murder Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the early Latino vote increased by 217 percent compared to 2022.

Polling by Pew Research Center in September and October found that a majority of Black (69 percent), Latino (67 percent), and Asian (66 percent) adults in the U.S. have a negative opinion of ICE, while 49 percent of white adults have an unfavorable view of the agency. Pew also found that Americans across racial and ethnic groups view ICE more unfavorably today than they did a year ago, with 56 percent of Americans saying they have a negative view of the agency overall. Only 35 percent say they view the agency favorably.

However, while voters demonstrated their rejection of ICE and Trump’s rule in Tuesday’s elections, it remains unclear if that will lead to sweeping policy changes. The mainstream Democratic Party position — touted by figures like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become Speaker of the House — is to call for reforms of ICE rather than the abolition of the agency. But human rights advocates have warned that reforms to ICE, like reforms to the police, will not quell the repression and brutality inherent to what is now the U.S.’s most well-funded law enforcement agency.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Indian Act controversy lingers more than a week after abolishment was raised in Ottawa
content:
Everyone, from pundits, constitutional lawyers and scholars to people in coffee shops and online, has been hashing out just what it could mean to abolish the Indian Act after it was raised by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew on Oct. 26 in Ottawa.


However, Kinew hasn’t provided context for his comment, which came out at what was the first First Nations First Ministers meeting in decades and touched off a firestorm of debate over what doing away with the controversial Act would actually do.


APTN News has reached out to Kinew’s office and requested an interview on several occasions, but those requests have been denied.


“We just had one of the most impactful meetings of the decade in Ottawa and everyone on social media is talking about the Indian Act and the complexities of whether or not it can be abolished and the problems if it is and all these different things, said Jennifer Laewetz, the CEO of Paskwâw Strategies, an Indigenous advisory firm in Saskatchewan. “It’s a little bit frustrating because we need to be united on a lot of other bigger issues right now.”


“I just really wish that our leaders would recognize sometimes that they have so much impact in these spaces that if you are going to say something as big as ‘you need to abolish the Indian Act’ you need to be prepared to follow up with people in Canada about what that looks like… and communicate how you see that happening exactly,” Laewetz said, appearing on

APTN News

 Truth and Politics on Friday.


Abolish the Indian Act. We have nothing to lose but our chains.


We will, of course, need new legislation that is an interface between the Federal government and First Nations. And this MUST be created alongside Chiefs and First Nation governments every step of the way. But it is time to move past the era of this outdated, racist, and patriarchal legislation.


I support Prime Minister Carney’s work to position Canada as a global leader in human rights and democracy. The Indian Act is inconsistent with achieving that vision.


Our laws at home should reflect the values we champion around the world.


It’s time for a relationship with First Nations people that reflects who we are as Canadians today, recognizes nationhood, and lives up to the true nature of reconciliation.


— Wab Kinew (@WabKinew)

October 26, 2026


In a video shared hundreds of thousands of times online, Kinew said, holding up his status card, that he thinks it’s time to abolish the Indian Act, calling it “long overdue.”


Kinew appeared in a weekly scheduled interview on CTV Winnipeg after making the comment, but has refused to respond to requests to elaborate on his pronouncement from APTN News.


Winnipeg Free Press columnist Niigaan Sinclair said on the same Truth and Politics episode that abolishment of the Indian Act would create a “vacuum.”


“The Indian Act is so deep,” Sinclair said, “it doesn’t just impact Indigenous People. The Indian Act impacts the Department of Agriculture, the RCMP…it impacts all the different ways we see property ownership in this country.


“This is something that is going to not just be a conversation about Indigenous Peoples, because we have to realize our rights don’t come from the Indian Act, even though Canada thinks…they come from the recognition within the Indian Act.”


Sinclair said most significantly, it would lead to a debate of Section 91(24) of the

Constitution Act, 1867

, which says that the federal government takes control of Indians and land reserved for Indians.


“We’ve been down that road and we know that constitutional debates end up in everybody under the sun talking about every single thing and everybody freaking out about referendums and separatism and Meech Lake and Charlottetown…,” Sincliar said.


“And if people aren’t radically running for the hills at this point, I would say its going to involve decades and definitely not something four-year governments can deal with directly.”

Honour of the Crown precludes talks of abolishment


The honour of the Crown, a foundational, unwritten constitutional principle in Canadian Law could halt any talks of abolishment before they start.


According to the

Centre for Constitutional Studies

Haida Nation

 and

Sparrow

author: El Surtidor
title: Como a quebra do banco Ueno, no Paraguai, acabou com o governo do presidente Santiago Peña
content:
Na terça-feira, 3 de novembro de 2026, quase 3 milhões de paraguaios — cerca de metade da população — acordaram sem poder usar o seu dinheiro.

 Às 3h24 da madrugada, o Banco Central do Paraguai (BCP) anunciou no X/Twitter o fechamento do Ueno Bank, banco digital ligado ao presidente Santiago Peña, por falta de solvência. As economias de milhares de famílias estavam depositadas ali, assim como 800 milhões de dólares em recursos públicos.


Naquele mesmo dia, o Ministério Público emitiu uma ordem de prisão contra oito dirigentes do banco, a partir de uma denúncia do Banco Central.

O principal apontado é Federico Miguel Vázquez, primeiro vice-presidente do Ueno e fundador e acionista majoritário do Grupo Vázquez

 — um conglomerado de pelo menos 28 empresas que fazem parte de um suposto esquema de captação de recursos e fraude bancária. O empresário está sendo apelidado de “Vorcaro do Paraguai”, pelas semelhanças com o escândalo brasileiro do

Banco Master

.


Na quarta-feira, 4 de novembro, o Ministério Público imputou a 27 dirigentes do grupo os crimes de conduta indevida em situações de crise e lesão de confiança, incluindo os oito primeiros. À tarde, deputados da oposição apresentaram o projeto de impeachment contra Peña e, nas ruas da capital, a polícia reprimiu manifestantes com balas de borracha, gás lacrimogêneo e caminhões-pipa.


Às 10h da manhã de quinta-feira, 5 de novembro, a Câmara dos Deputados deu início ao processo de impeachment para destituir o presidente. Mas, às 13h30, Peña renunciou antes que fosse afastado. O Senado tentou aceitar sua renúncia, mas prevaleceu a linha do impeachment, que continua nesta sexta-feira. Paralelamente, um juiz decidiu pela prisão preventiva dos oito dirigentes do Ueno.


Na mesma manhã de quinta-feira, senadores da oposição apresentaram uma denúncia contra Peña ao Ministério Público especializado em crimes econômicos, o mesmo que investiga os dirigentes do Ueno Bank. “Que ele seja indiciado e tenha seus bens confiscados. O dinheiro que roubaram precisa ser recuperado e usado para pagar as pessoas”, afirmou a senadora oposicionista Esperanza Martínez. A denúncia também inclui integrantes da diretoria do BCP, como Carlos Carvallo Spalding, que foi dirigente do Ueno Bank antes de assumir a presidência do Banco Central durante o governo Peña.


Se a investigação do Ministério Público comprovar os crimes atribuídos aos dirigentes do Ueno e do Grupo Vázquez, assim como a cumplicidade de Santiago Peña e de integrantes do BCP, esse caso será tão grave quanto ou maior que o do Banco Master, no Brasil

, ligado a

Flávio Bolsonaro

 e que afetou quase 2 milhões de brasileiros. Há, além disso, um temor latente de aprofundamento de uma crise social e econômica, com diversas ramificações a médio e longo prazo.


Miguel Vázquez, executivo do banco Ueno, está em prisão preventiva


As manobras que permitiram um esquema de fraude com recursos públicos


O crescimento do Ueno Bank e do Grupo Vázquez foi meteórico. Em menos de cinco anos, o grupo alcançou uma carteira de milhões de clientes.

Mas esse aumento contou com o apoio do poder político a partir da chegada de Santiago Peña à presidência, em agosto de 2023.

 Desde então, diversas manobras legais e políticas permitiram a expansão desse grupo econômico:


Manipulação das normas do Instituto de Previdência Social em benefício do banco Ueno.


Três meses depois da posse de Peña, o jornal ABC Color denunciou que o conselho da instituição de seguridade social havia

reduzido

 as exigências para que um banco pudesse receber seus recursos, o que permitiu que o Ueno se qualificasse. Um ano depois, também foi eliminado o limite patrimonial que o IPS podia depositar em um banco.


O Ueno ficou com cerca de 350 milhões de dólares do Fundo Comum de Aposentadorias e Pensões, aproximadamente 9% do dinheiro dos aposentados atuais e futuros. Agora, com o fechamento do banco, não se sabe qual será o destino desse dinheiro nem por quais mecanismos ele poderá ser recuperado.


Alteração da lei de conflitos de interesses e das portas giratórias


No final de 2023, o Congresso enfraqueceu a lei de conflitos de interesses, o que

facilitou

 a nomeação de ex-funcionários do banco Ueno e do Banco Basa — do ex-presidente Horacio Cartes — para cargos estratégicos na economia, além da distribuição de licitações ao Grupo Vázquez, no qual Peña tinha ações.

content:
By John Amidon, World BEYOND War, November 6, 2026

title: Latino Voters Just Remade the Political Map
content:
The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago voted for Democrats in large numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate. Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in an historic victory, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Democratic Latino governors.

“Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state,” says Democracy Now! co-host Juan Gonzalez. “Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latino voters towards Democrats in state after state. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago swung to Democrats in huge numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate.

Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in historic victories, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Latinx Democratic governors. On Tuesday night, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa defeated the incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott with a margin of over 700,000 votes. This is a clip from her speech.

GOV.-ELECT GINA HINOJOSA: I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaking in Austin, Texas, right after she was declared the winner.

And this is California Governor-elect Xavier Becerra addressing supporters Tuesday night in Sacramento after he easily defeated Republican challenger Steve Hilton.

GOV.-ELECT XAVIER BECERRA: Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era. Tonight, I have a message for all those who have been made to feel afraid. There’s a new sheriff in town, and he’s got a law degree and a union card. If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight.

AMY GOODMAN: For more on the significance of these victories, we turn to Juan González, yes, co-host of Democracy Now!, author of, among other books, Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America.

Juan, can you talk about this massive Latino victory across the country? What was expected? What wasn’t expected?

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, well, Amy, it’s been quite a week in U.S. politics, and I’ve been poring over the voting returns and the exit polls the past two days to glean a clearer sense of the trends and outcomes that maybe the major media may have missed, and not just about Latinos.

Let’s begin with the turnout, which I believe is always key. It tells you how motivated and mobilized people were. Well, nationally, the turnout was 63% of registered voters. Now, that’s high by historic standards for a midterm, because, remember, it’s always less voting in the midterms. But it’s still a lower rate than either the Biden midterm election of 2022 or the first Trump midterm elections of 2018. So, while some areas of the country may have had a historic turnout, across the country this was not the highest turnout of any midterm in recent years.

And the most notable shift occurred among white voters. They made up 73% of all ballots cast. That’s the same percentage that they made in 2022. But while they voted 58% for Republicans four years ago — and I’m comparing it midterm to midterm, not midterm to the presidential election — this time they split almost evenly between Republicans and Democrats. So you’re talking a huge shift among white voters away from the Republican Party and to the Democratic Party.

author: Ohood Nassar
title: “The Hall Turned Red”: Survivors Recount Israeli Strike on University in Gaza
content:
“I still remember the bombing, the sound of people screaming, and the sight of the injured,” said one student.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

At 10:15 am on October 25, 2026, an Israeli missile struck the courtyard in front of the female students’ lecture hall at Gaza’s Islamic University. Baraa Abu Hujeir, a 22-year-old English language student, was attending a linguistics lecture inside.

“We were in the linguistics lecture hall when we were suddenly hit by the blast. Stones scattered around us, and pieces of the windows, which were made of nylon and wood, flew toward us,” Abu Hujeir told me.

She confirmed that approximately 130 female students were inside the hall, along with their lecturer, Dr. Khader Khader.

Minutes before the strike, Abu Hujeir had been absorbed in the lecture despite the difficult conditions under which the university was attempting to continue teaching.

“I was excited, and the lecture was very interesting, despite the lack of resources. There was no electricity, no internet, and not even a blackboard,” she said.

Getting to the university was not easy for Abu Hujeir, who lives with her family in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza. She spent around half an hour looking for transportation before making the 40-minute journey to the university.

During the lecture, she was reading the presentation slides on Dr. Khader’s laptop when everything suddenly changed.

“As I was reading the slides, the hall turned red, and stones scattered around us,” she said.

According to Abu Hujeir, there had been no warning before the explosion. As the blast rang out, the students began screaming. Dr. Khader’s laptop and Abu Hujeir’s own iPad were damaged.

But what frightened her most was seeing her classmate Salwa injured in the face: “Her face was covered in blood,” Abu Hujeir recalled.

At first, Abu Hujeir thought the missile had struck the lecture hall itself. She and the other students went outside to see what had happened and discovered that the missile had landed directly in front of the hall, approximately one meter away, according to her account.

Fear quickly spread among the students, especially when they began hearing calls for the university to be evacuated immediately amid concerns that it could be attacked again.

Dr. Khader, 80, was inside the linguistics lecture hall explaining the lesson when the strike transformed the room into a scene of panic and confusion.

After the explosion, he called for the university to be evacuated immediately. However, he refused to leave the hall until he had made sure that all the female students had evacuated safely.

Abu Hujeir says she tried to take his hand to help him leave, but he refused and told her, “You leave.”

As he prepared to evacuate, Dr. Khader saw that his car, which he had parked outside the entrance to the lecture hall, had been damaged by the strike. Its windows were shattered, and its tires were damaged. He stood looking at it sadly, tears in his eyes, repeating, “My car is gone.”

After leaving the hall, Abu Hujeir found more than six injured people outside, their bodies covered in blood. Among the injured was her 18-year-old classmate, Ahmed Nasser.

Nasser had been waiting on the steps outside the female students’ lecture hall for Dr. Khader so he could help him move to the male students’ lecture hall. During the war, Dr. Khader had sustained an injury to his foot that left him unable to move independently. He needed someone to hold his hand and assist him when walking.

But the explosion struck before Nasser could help his professor.

“At the moment of the attack, I was sitting on the steps outside the girls’ lecture hall, waiting for the doctor. When the explosion happened, I fell to the ground and couldn’t run,” Nasser told me.

His fear was compounded by his inability to move and his uncertainty about the extent of his injuries.

“I couldn’t run, so I was screaming and crying,” he said, his voice breaking. “I thought I had been paralyzed and would lose my ability to move.”

Nasser’s back was bleeding. His university classmates tried to provide first aid, using a piece of cloth to stop the bleeding before he was transferred to Al-Quds Hospital in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City. He had lost consciousness by the time he reached the hospital.

The first strike was not the end of the violence at the Islamic …

author: Mark Olalde
title: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Is Invested in AI Industry
content:
Other officials across the administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Trump administration has likened the need to build out the nation’s artificial intelligence infrastructure to the Manhattan Project, the World War II effort that produced the world’s first atomic bomb.

The White House’s point person on the effort, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, has spoken of the “AI arms race” with China as an existential issue for the nation. “AI is manufacturing intelligence, and, if we don’t manufacture more intelligence than our adversaries, it affects every job, every company and every industry,” he said during his Senate confirmation hearing in January 2025.

But advancing the administration’s AI objectives also could benefit Burgum’s own finances.

Much of his wealth is held in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, according to his 2026 financial disclosure form, which has not been previously reported. Between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those investments are in AI companies, according to an analysis of the companies’ marketing materials shared with ProPublica by public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks. (Government financial disclosure forms allow filers to report wide ranges instead of the specific value of their investments.)

Burgum made his fortune 25 years ago when he sold a software company to Microsoft and has remained heavily invested in technology. In the year before joining the administration, when he was North Dakota’s governor, he made between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, Save Our Parks’ analysis showed. In 2025, he sold millions of dollars of stocks and equity in AI companies, bringing in capital gains worth between $2.5 million and $15.1 million.

In the ethics agreement Burgum signed as part of his Senate confirmation, he agreed to resign from his positions at Arthur but not give up his financial interests there.

“Secretary Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations,” a U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson told ProPublica in a statement. “Any suggestion that his office decisions are driven by personal investments are false and completely unsupported.”

Officials across the Trump administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers. For example, 380 of President Donald Trump’s political appointees or their spouses hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia, which has become the world’s most valuable company thanks to the data center boom. More than 320 have ties to Alphabet, Google’s parent company, which plans to spend at least $195 billion this year building data centers and AI-related technology. And more than 240 are invested in or otherwise have financial ties to Meta Platforms, which is developing a “fleet” of data centers. This is according to an analysis of records added last week to the Trump Team Financials database developed by ProPublica to make accessible the financial disclosures of administration officials.

Federal officials’ activities are governed by a criminal statute that sets a high burden of proof for potential wrongdoing — for example, approving permits for a company in which they are substantially invested, multiple ethics professors and lawyers told ProPublica. They said that Burgum’s investments appear to be acceptable under this law.

But ethics rules that do not carry criminal penalties also apply, explained Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog group. These rules, she said, “instruct officials not to work on anything that would create the appearance of a conflict of interest.” She said this would include Burgum’s support for data centers on federal land while holding investments in AI.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and President George W. Bush’s chief ethics lawyer, agreed that Burgum should avoid making decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. “I, as the ethics lawyer, would insist he stay away from it,” Painter said. “In the Bush administration, the answer would’ve been ‘he has to recuse,’ I can guarantee you that.”

author: Michael Arria
title: The GOP Wasn’t the Only Midterms Loser. Voters Slapped Data Centers With Limits.
content:
This week voters nationwide approved 40 out of the 41 ballot measures that had been proposed to rein in data centers.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

In recent months, thousands of Americans have flooded municipal government buildings to testify against the construction of AI data centers in their communities.

According to a May 2026 Gallup poll, 7 out of 10 people oppose the construction of data centers in their local area, citing grave concerns over their environmental impact, water consumption, noise, and potential health risks. A Blue Rose Research poll from December 2025 found that Americans would rather live near prisons or nuclear power plants than data centers.

“Overcoming this opposition stands as a major hurdle in the expansion of AI computing,” noted Gallup Senior Editor Jeffrey M. Jones. “The intensity of opposition means that proposed data centers are likely to spur grassroots activism from local residents as well as legal challenges.”

Many of those challenges have proven successful, as more than 500 jurisdictions have approved moratoriums or bans even before the midterms. That trend was extended during this week’s elections, where data center-related questions appeared on the ballot in 13 states: 40 out of 41 ballot measures placing restrictions on data centers were passed throughout the country.

Data center-related questions appeared on the ballot in 13 states.

In many cases, the results were not close: 77 percent of voters in Edgewater, Florida, approved a ban on new data centers, while 82 percent of voters in Alhambra, California, endorsed one. Ohio, which had more data center-related questions on its ballots than any other state, saw voters pass outright bans in 11 municipalities, while another seven approved further regulations on them.

“Tuesday’s election was a historically bad night for the Republican Party,” declared the Boston Globe. “It might have been even worse for big tech and their plans to spend trillions of dollars building AI data centers.”

Anger over data centers certainly wasn’t limited to local ballot questions. Polling suggests that it helped determine the results of major races amid the Democratic Party’s historic “blue wave.” Exit polling from NBC News reveals that 56 percent of voters identified data centers and AI as a “crucial or major factor” in their vote.

Chief among these contests was the Ohio Senate race, where incumbent Republican Sen. John Husted was ousted by Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Husted was backed by powerful tech giants like Oracle’s Larry Ellison and Safra Catz; and a cryptocurrency PAC, funded by companies like Coinbase, spent $55 million trying to stomp out Brown’s challenge.

The Brown campaign consistently highlighted these ties during the campaign, running ads that referred to Husted as “the face of data centers in Ohio” and bankrolling billboards that directed voters to a website which details how Husted is the “chief reason” that 226 data centers exist in the state.

An internal National Republican Senatorial Committee memo, originally reported on by Axios, showed that Brown’s attacks were working and causing Republican anxiety over not just the Ohio race, but the GOP’s relationship with data centers more broadly.

“More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” it read. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”

56 percent of voters identified data centers and AI as a “crucial or major factor” in their vote.

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a data center moratorium, ousted Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. Abbott embraced guardrails on the facilities leading up to the election, but for years he welcomed their construction in the state and, in 2025, he declared Texas to be the “epicenter of AI development.”

“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist who works on AI, told WIRED.

author: Jan Daalder
title: Queimaduras, terror psicológico e salários atrasados em data centers na Europa
content:
Sandu Dumitrescu* olhou para o relógio. Ele estava terminando os últimos 15 minutos de seu turno em uma obra de data center do Google em Saint Ghislain, Bélgica, em março, quando recebeu uma ligação. Tinha acabado de realizar verificações elétricas nos ventiladores do

hall

 quando seu gerente comunicou um pedido final: fazer dois testes rápidos antes de sair.


O funcionário de 34 anos já havia trabalhado quase 10 horas. No ambiente altamente pressurizado de GBL-6, o sexto data center Google em um vasto campus avaliado em 5 bilhões de euros, pedidos de última hora como esse eram normais.


“Eu não tinha escolha”, diz Sandu. “Pessoas foram demitidas por dizer não.” Ele acreditava que os supervisores no local, da empresa irlandesa Dornan Engineering, não aceitariam bem uma recusa. Como ele dependia de seu contrato semanal, e tinha esperanças de conseguir ligar para sua esposa e filho pequeno na Romênia naquela noite, decidiu executar o trabalho.


Era uma tarefa que ele havia feito muitas vezes antes e envolvia uma série de testes para medir a segurança e integridade da fiação elétrica. Era para ter levado cerca de uma hora. Sandu diz que o pedido lhe foi feito verbalmente, por um intermediário. Um traje protetor estava guardado em uma sala de equipamentos. Ir ao ocal para buscá-lo teria adicionado mais 15 minutos ao trabalho, diz ele, e havia pessoas esperando.

Na pressa, Sandu decidiu não ir pegar o traje.


Na sala de tensão, Sandu diz que os gerentes confirmaram que as linhas haviam sido desenergizadas. Na primeira rodada, tudo correu conforme o planejado. Mas, no segundo teste, enquanto segurava uma pinça isolada, ele conectou os cabos. Mas desta vez, os cabos de energia estavam ligados.


A explosão foi imediata e catastrófica. Em milissegundos, 400 volts e 12 mil amperes atingiram o rosto de Sandu e atravessaram o lado direito de seu corpo. Um colega que estava embaixo da plataforma e presenciou o incidente contou à

Investigate Europe

 ter “ouvido um barulho alto, muita fumaça e o visto [Sandu] gritando de dor”.


“Fiquei completamente cego”, relembra Sandu. “Disse aos gerentes três vezes que não conseguia enxergar. Mas nenhum deles respondeu”, diz ele. De acordo com a testemunha que procurou ajuda – enquanto desembaraçava Sandu dos cabos com seu corpo queimado – os gerentes fugiram, ao passo que Sandu se contorcia de dor no chão.


Trabalhadores se apressaram para levar Sandu para a ambulância. Quando os médicos o receberam no Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, ele foi colocado em coma induzido por cinco dias.


Registros hospitalares acessados pela

Investigate Europe

 mostram que o choque havia queimado 12% do corpo de Sandu, com queimaduras de segundo grau no rosto e pescoço, além de queimaduras de terceiro grau no ombro direito e nos dedos. Fotografias mostram orelhas queimadas e lábios inchados e em carne viva, com o braço cheio de hematomas e pele coagulada.


Quando Sandu acordou na unidade de tratamento intensivo uma semana depois da cirurgia, sua mulher estava à beira de sua cama. Ele diz que todo o seu corpo parecia uma “bolha branca e escaldante… Era tanta dor. O coração humano não consegue compreender”, relembra.


Sandu fotografado em outubro de 2026, meses depois de a eletrocussão por arco elétrico ter queimado 12% do seu corpo


Dois dias após acordar do coma, representantes do Google, da irlandesa Dornan e de uma agência de recrutamento holandesa, a Wanted, vieram visitá-lo. Sandu diz que enquanto estava deitado em uma maca de hospital, enfaixado, Google e Dornan tomaram declarações dele sobre o acidente. Segundo Sandu,

o funcionário do Google lhe disse que tinha sorte de estar vivo.


A descarga elétrica sofrida por Sandu foi brutal e assustadora.

Até hoje, porém, não há registro de nenhuma multa ou sanção pelo incidente.

 Inspetores federais do trabalho na Bélgica encerraram sua investigação sobre o acidente no final de outubro e não encontraram irregularidades. Sandu diz que nunca foi entrevistado diretamente pelas autoridades trabalhistas.


Apesar de ter pedido o relatório sobre seu acidente à Wanted e ao Google, ele ainda não recebeu o documento. Um mês após o acidente, o recrutador enviou uma mensagem a Sandu perguntando como estava. E perguntaram:

“[A empresa] está recrutando mais testadores (talvez você conheça pessoas?)”.

author: Daron Letts
title: Experts decry Nunavut’s ‘Band-Aid’ approach to foster care
content:
The broken child welfare system in Nunavut is rooted in the territorial government’s colonial approach to the problem, say some with years of experience with the system.


“The taking of Indigenous children never stopped at residential school,” said Jeremy Young, who was separated from his mother as a child. “It only continued with foster care.”


Young spoke to Nunatsiaq News about his experience in Nunavut’s foster care system Thursday in response to the latest

report

 by the federal auditor general

 i

nto the territorial government’s handling of youth in its care.


Tuesday’s report, the fifth over 15 years, shows little has changed. The Nunavut government is failing to account for the number of children in its care, failing to do consistent check-ins and failing in its duty to make sure every foster child is put into an appropriate home.


Young, now 26 years old, was taken from his mother as a child in Pangnirtung even though she did her best, Young said.


He blamed overcrowding and poverty for his family’s situation, saying his mother tried for 12 years to get housing for her family but ultimately could not.


“Society has failed Indigenous people,” he said. “That’s why we live in poverty. That’s why we go through the traumas we went through.”


Young believes Inuit self-government is the antidote to the problems in the foster care system.


Rankin Inlet researcher and academic Peter Williamson and Arlene Hache, an advocate with decades of experience working with Indigenous women agree.


Williamson said even if the territorial government finally heeds the auditor general’s

recommendations

 for fixing foster care, which includes

getting a handle

 on its own information management system, it wouldn’t solve the root causes that lead to the removal of children from their families? It would only streamline the system.


“They are identifying the Band-Aid solutions in government instead of fixing the root causes in the communities,” Williamson said.


Unstable housing, low education, unemployment and poverty are risk factors for removing children from their families, Williamson said, citing peer-reviewed studies by North American and Nordic researchers.


“Those are prevalent in Nunavut,” he said.


Mothers forced to enter emergency housing have an even greater risk of having their children taken from them, he added.


Hache agreed, calling the current system a form of “genocide” of Indigenous people.


“When [government workers] go into a family or a community, they are searching for all these problems,” she said. “Because of their colonial mindset and their racism.”


An alternative is an Inuit-led, community-based model that “supports families, recognizes their value and their ability to recover, and provides support, mentorship, and training,” she said.


“Let’s persuade people that they can grow from the place they are to a new place. That’s how elders in Inuit communities think.”


Shortly after the territory’s inception in 1999, the Nunavut government invited Hache on a territory-wide tour to share information about this approach to foster care, she said.


It wasn’t a new idea. Developed and adopted in Hawaii in 1979, it is still in use today.


“It was a well-evidenced model based on world-Indigenous understandings of families and children,” Hache said. “It wasn’t like it was radical or new. But everything in the North is radical and new if it’s not colonial.”


Nunavut rejected the model.

author: Sophia Sheera
title: UK Government to Extend Palantir’s NHS Contract by Two Years
content:
The government is planning to extend spytech firm Palantir’s £330m deal with the NHS despite pressure from Labour MPs, medical unions and activists to cut ties with the company. 


Ministers had the option of triggering a break clause in the contract in February. However, a review concluded that removing Palantir and switching providers within four months would be too disruptive,

the FT reported

, with ministers drawing up plans to potentially replace it with a British alternative in two years’ time instead. 


Tech justice campaign group

Foxglove said

 this decision showed “a serious ignorance” of Palantir’s contract, which “specifically requires the firm to provide bridging support for up to 24 months if the contract is ended” to ensure continuity of service.


“The reported claim that it would not be ‘practical to replace Palantir within the next four months’ is, frankly, nonsense,” said Foxglove’s head of communications Tom Hegarty.


The decision comes amid growing opposition to Palantir’s involvement in British public services. The firm has faced criticism over its work with the Trump administration and the Israeli military, while its co-founder Peter Thiel has previously attacked the NHS.


Last week, it was revealed that dozens of UK hospitals reportedly benefitting from a platform built by Palantir are

not even using it

.


Novara Media also revealed a fortnight ago that British MPs who have criticised Palantir in parliament

received intimidating letters

 from the firm. 


Amnesty International’s UK crisis campaigner Tom Guha said: “Patients, healthcare workers and campaigners have pushed ministers to look for a way out of this contract. Ministers must show Palantir the door now, not give it two more years to bed in further.


“Palantir has publicly acknowledged supporting Israel’s military in ‘war-related missions’,” he added. “Any company linked to genocide has no place in our NHS.”

author: Chris Walker
title: Newsom Commutes All 548 Death Sentences in California
content:
The governor altered the sentences of people facing the death penalty to lifetime imprisonment without parole.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On Thursday, California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom announced the commutation of 548 death sentences, reducing the sentence of everyone on the state’s death row to life without parole.

California has more people sentenced to capital punishment than any other state, but for years there has been a moratorium on carrying out the death penalty. Newsom’s action ensures that the moratorium is permanent for those 548 individuals.

The action doesn’t abolish the death penalty in the state, meaning that future convictions could result in death sentences. It also commutes all capital punishment sentences to lifetime imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that ensures these individuals will still face death by incarceration.

But the move is being praised as a step in the right direction — one that could result in other states following suit.

Newsom said that he made the decision to commute the sentences of everyone on death row “because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”

“I have decided to commute every death sentence,” he said.

Understanding that his action would be criticized, Newsom elaborated on why he could not go case-by-case to decide whether one person was deserving of commutation while others were not, writing:

Some have said I should not grant clemency to people who committed the ‘worst of the worst’ crimes. I carefully considered different categories of capital crimes and offender characteristics. I have learned, however, from speaking with the victims harmed by these crimes, that each experiences their loss as the worst of the worst. I have concluded that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims.

The governor concluded he had to “issue the same commutation to every condemned person,” and commuted death penalty sentences to “life without the possibility of parole.”

“These offenders will die in prison,” Newsom acknowledged, “but not by our hand.”

Newsom’s decision is not final for about half of those it affects — by state law, commutations where a person has multiple felony convictions require a review by the state Supreme Court, and could result in legal challenges

Families of victims are split on the matter. Some have expressed anger over the action taken by Newsom, while others have said they encouraged him to move forward with the decision in conversations over the past month.

“We used to think that having a vengeful death penalty sentence is going to be what gave us justice. We’ve discovered that it doesn’t,” said Jess Nichol, whose sister was killed by someone who received a commutation from Newsom.

Human rights organizations are celebrating Newsom’s action.

“We are grateful that Gov. Newsom, like other Republican and Democratic leaders across the country, has decided to grant clemency to individuals on death row,” said Laura Porter, executive director of the U.S. Campaign to End the Death Penalty. “The historic number of commuted sentences would set a new record and offer an acknowledgment that the death penalty process is flawed.”

“This is a day that will be remembered in California’s history and resonate globally for years to come,” said Amnesty International USA’s executive director Nadia Daar, adding:

The death penalty should be abolished, everywhere. Today marks a significant moment for human rights in California and across the country, but it is not the finishing line. The world is watching, and this decision is showing that progress is possible, and the United States, which remains among a small group of countries that continues to carry out executions, can move beyond the death penalty.

Yasmin Cader, deputy executive director of Program, Strategy, and Culture for the ACLU, also heralded Newsom’s action.

“This marks a historic step toward ending the death penalty across the United States. … California has turned the page on a systemic injustice and set a powerful example for leaders across the country to follow,” Cader said.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “En esta causa alguien tiene que caer”: las presiones a un policía que declaró en el juicio por la golpiza a jóvenes Qom
content:
Un efectivo denunció que recibió amenazas de sanciones y sumarios por parte de sus superiores cuando debía declarar sobre el allanamiento ilegal y brutal golpiza perpetradas por un grupo de uniformados contra jóvenes de la comunidad Qom de Fontana, Chaco, en mayo de 2020. En la sexta audiencia también declaró un comisario retirado que identificó a varios de los imputados en los registros audiovisuales incorporados al expediente.


La frase expone una arista hasta ahora no conocida del juicio por la golpiza y los hechos de violencia institucional sufridos por integrantes de la comunidad Qom en el barrio Banderas Argentinas de Fontana: las presuntas presiones dentro de la propia fuerza policial para condicionar testimonios durante la investigación. “En esta causa alguien tiene que caer”, habría sido la advertencia que recibió uno de los efectivos que declaró ante el tribunal.


El episodio salió a la luz durante la sexta audiencia del juicio oral y público, realizada el martes, en la que prestaron declaración dos policías que se desempeñaban en Fontana cuando ocurrieron los hechos, en mayo de 2020. Uno de ellos, el oficial principal Héctor Ariel Velázquez, denunció que sus superiores lo amenazaron con sanciones y actuaciones sumariales cuando debía aportar información sobre el procedimiento investigado.


La jornada también dejó otro aporte relevante para la reconstrucción de lo sucedido: el comisario retirado Orlando Ismael Trangoni, quien era segundo jefe de la Comisaría Tercera, reconoció en los registros audiovisuales a varios de los efectivos que hoy están sentados en el banquillo de los acusados.


Las presiones 


Velázquez fue el primero en declarar. En 2020 prestaba servicios en la Comisaría Segunda de Fontana y había intervenido en actuaciones vinculadas con los hechos que ahora se juzgan.


Durante su exposición manifestó tener dificultades para recordar distintos detalles de los procedimientos, una situación que atribuyó a la cantidad de intervenciones policiales en las que había participado. Sin embargo, el interrogatorio dejó al descubierto contradicciones entre sus respuestas ante el tribunal y la declaración que había brindado el 13 de octubre de 2020.


En aquella oportunidad, el efectivo había identificado a integrantes de la fuerza a partir de los registros audiovisuales que hoy forman parte del expediente. Ese antecedente fue confrontado durante la audiencia con sus actuales manifestaciones.


En ese contexto, Velázquez reveló que había recibido presiones de sus superiores cuando debía prestar declaración ante mandos policiales. Según relató, lo amenazaron con sanciones y la apertura de actuaciones sumariales.


Entre los superiores que mencionó se encuentran el comisario mayor Godoy y el comisario Ariel Alejandro Gonzalo González. El testigo describió el mensaje que, según sostuvo, le transmitieron en aquella instancia: “En esta causa alguien tiene que caer”.


La denuncia abre un interrogante sobre el comportamiento de la propia estructura policial durante la investigación y las condiciones en las que se recogieron los testimonios de los efectivos que podían aportar información sobre el operativo.


Reconoció a los policías


El segundo testimonio correspondió a Trangoni, quien se desempeñaba como segundo jefe de la Comisaría Tercera de Fontana al momento de los hechos. Al comenzar, manifestó desconocer los motivos precisos de su citación y expresó dificultades para recordar distintos aspectos del procedimiento.


No obstante, la exhibición de los registros audiovisuales incorporados a la causa permitió avanzar en la identificación de los policías que participaron de los operativos, tanto en la vivienda como dentro de la dependencia.


A partir de esas imágenes, el excomisario reconoció a Diego Adrián Latorre, Orlando Sergio Martín Cabrera, Cristian Eduardo Foschiatti, Cristian Benítez, Cristian Borda y Marcelo Eduardo Blanco. También identificó a Sofía González, a quien señaló como responsable de la guardia.


Trangoni reconoció, además, las maniobras utilizadas por el personal policial para trasladar a las personas aprehendidas hacia el interior de la comisaría.


Otro tramo de su declaración estuvo relacionado con los protocolos que deben aplicarse cuando una persona detenida presenta lesiones. En ese sentido, ratificó que, conforme a las normas de actuación policial y a la Ley de Seguridad Pública, corresponde trasladar inmediatamente a toda persona lesionada a Sanidad Policial.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Radio Encuentro denunció judicialmente al ENACOM
content:
Fue a través de un amparo presentado en el juzgado federal de Viedma, Río Negro, donde el medio comunitario integrante de FARCO señaló las deudas por parte del Ente Nacional de Comunicaciones (ENaCom) en el marco del incumplimiento de la Ley de Servicios de Comunicación Audiovisual.


Escuchar la entrevista a Nestor Busso de Radio Encuentro en el Informativo FARCO


 


La presentación judicial exige que se ordene al ente el inmediato cumplimiento de las obligaciones de pago asumidas en el marco del Fondo de Fomento Concursable para Medios de Comunicación Audiovisual (FOMECA).


En este caso el organismo nacional le debe a la emisora $3.700.000 correspondientes a los segundos desembolsos de los tres subsidios adjudicados en el marco de la Línea Gestión de Medios (Línea M/2023, Sublínea Audiovisual) y de la Línea Producciones (Línea P/2023, formatos Programa o Informativo Diario de Radio y Programa o Informativo Diario de Televisión).


En la presentación, Radio Encuentro asegura que los segundos desembolsos nunca fueron pagados.


Escuchar la entrevista a Emilia Calderón, presidenta de FARCO


Emilia Calderón, presidenta de FARCO, señaló que “el amparo pone en términos jurídicos algo que venimos denunciando hace más de 2 años que tiene que ver con el incumplimiento del stado con los medios comunitarios”.


De esta manera, Calderón señaló que FARCO acompaña la decisión de denunciar los incumplimientos del estado en reiteradas ocasiones, con un ente intervenido desde los comienzos del gobierno del presidente Javier Milei.


Si bien la administración estatal asumió que

retenía miles de millones de pesos

 de fondos no adjudicados, continúa sin dar demasiadas explicaciones. La información fue confirmada a través de un pedido de acceso a la información pública que realizó Juan Salvador Delú, vice presidente de FARCO,  a mediados del 2024. Hasta el momento se desconoce el destino de los fondos concursables cobrados y no ejecutados que por ley corresponden a los medios comunitarios.


Emilia Calderón, también remarcó: “FOMECA no es una ayuda económica que el gobierno puede decidir si entrega o no, es una política establecida por la ley  que define este porcentaje de los recursos con un destino específico”.


En comunicación con el informativo FARCO, Nestor Busso, de Radio Encuentro recordó: “Hemos reclamado de diversas formas, pedido entrevistas con funcionarios, hemos enviado solicitudes formales de pronto despacho, hemos enviado carta de documento y no tuvimos respuestas, entonces iniciamos una demanda judicial”.


Además del pedido de acceso a la información, en julio del 2025 las radios que integran FARCO realizaron presentaciones de cartas documento contra el organismo que no obtuvieron respuesta del ENACOM.


“Desde FARCO estamos reclamando que se cumpla la ley, que se paguen las deudas, que exista una política pública de fomento que garantice la continuidad”-

 Emilia Calderón

. 


Cientos de medios comunitarios y populares se encuentran en la misma situación que Radio Encuentro. “También es el caso de otras emisoras”, dijo Nestor Busso, “son proyectos que ya se concursaron, se ganaron, se firmaron convenios para su ejecución, se rindieron los primeros desembolsos, se ejecutó la totalidad del proyecto y el Gobierno no pagó”.


“Lo que ya habíamos anunciado a través de pedido de pronto despacho del documento al interventor del ENACOM, ahora lo hacemos a través de esta demanda judicial que está patrocinando un abogado de La Plata, Jerónimo Guerrero Iraola” finalizó Busso.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: 2026 Midterms Set New Record for Women Governors, With Historic Firsts Across the Country
content:
The 2026 midterm elections marked a historic breakthrough for women’s representation in state leadership, with voters electing women governors in record numbers and breaking longstanding barriers for women of color. From Georgia to New Mexico, several candidates made history as the first women, Black women, Native American women, and Latina women to lead their states.

In 2027, at least 17 women will serve as governors, representing at least 34% of all governors nationwide. This surpasses the previous record of 14 women governors. This year, 15 women won gubernatorial elections, including 12 Democrats and three Republicans. Two women remain in gubernatorial contests that are too close to call in Alaska and Kansas as of November 5.

Among the most significant victories was Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will become Georgia’s first woman governor and the first Black woman elected governor of any state. The former Atlanta mayor defeated businessman Rick Jackson, ending more than two decades of Republican control of the governor’s office. Bottoms’ victory represents a historic milestone for Black women, who have long been underrepresented in the nation’s highest state offices.

In New Mexico, Deb Haaland will become the first Native American woman governor in US history. A member of the Pueblo of Laguna, Haaland previously served as an US representative and as secretary of the Interior under the Biden administration, becoming the first Native American to lead a federal executive department. Her election also marks another milestone for New Mexico, which elected an all women of color gubernatorial ticket with Lieutenant Governor-elect Stephanie Garcia Richard.

Women also broke barriers in several states that had never elected a woman governor. Amy Klobuchar will become Minnesota’s first woman governor after defeating Lisa Demuth. In Ohio, Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor, defeating Vivek Ramaswamy. Although Nancy Hollister briefly served as Ohio’s governor through succession in 1998, Acton will be the first woman elected directly to the office.

In Tennessee, Marsha Blackburn will become the state’s first woman governor after defeating Jerri Green. Her victory marks another first for a state that has never elected a woman to its highest executive office.

The election also brought historic representation for Latina women. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott to become Texas’ first Latina governor. Hinojosa’s election also represents a significant political shift in a state where Republicans have held the governorship for more than three decades.

Beyond these historic firsts, women secured victories and retained governorships across the country. Women governors will continue leading states including Arizona, Arkansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, New York, Oregon and Rhode Island, among others. Their victories demonstrate the growing presence of women in state executive leadership across party lines.

Despite this progress, women remain underrepresented in gubernatorial offices. Even with the record number of women entering office in 2027, they will hold about one-third of the nation’s governorships. According to CAWP, 14 states will still have never had a woman governor.

This election highlights the importance of women’s representation in elected office, particularly for women who have historically faced barriers to political leadership. While these victories do not eliminate the structural inequalities that continue to limit women’s political participation, they mark meaningful progress. Women showed up and broke barriers, and it’s only just the beginning.
